tropes.html: Tony does this during his raid on Gulmira. Several terrorists use the villagers as human shields to force Tony to stand down. Fortunately he has some form of shoulder mounted guns that can target and take down the terrorists before they can harm their hostages.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Collected in a subpage for the Iron Man series.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: In the scene where Stark rides in the Funvee, the driver makes a point of the fact that she is an Airman, not a Soldier. As the markings on the exterior of the humvee show, the three airmen are United States Air Forces Security Forces airmen, whose duties include base security, convoy escort, and ground combat. As it happens, all four branches of the US military have their own ground combat personnel of varying numbers and quality, and all four branches enforce Insistent Terminology when it comes to what you call them (Army has Soldiers, Air Force has Airmen, Navy has Sailors, and Marine Corps has Marines)note This insistence is even present within the same branch; in the Navy, for example, a "pilot" is someone who controls a ship. Someone who flies a plane is called an "aviator".

tropes.name: Skewed Priorities
tropes.html: Upon returning to America after three months in terrorist captivity, Tony insists on first getting an American cheeseburger and hold a company press conference rather than go to the hospital.

tropes.name: Skipping the Basics
tropes.html:
As soon as Tony has gotten the Iron Man Mk.II flight-capable, he immediately sets out on a test flight to push it to its limits and try to break the SR-52 Blackbird's altitude limit, without trying to get the hang of it first. He nearly crashes multiple times, encounters an icing problem at high altitude that almost causes him to fatally plummet to Earth, and upon arriving back at his house and shutting off the thrusters, the weight sends him plummeting through multiple stories. Some of these teething problems come in handy during the climactic battle against Obadiah Stane's Iron Monger.
Iron Man: JARVIS, sometimes you gotta learn to run before you can learn to walk.

tropes.name: Slap-Slap-Kiss
tropes.html:
Christine Everhart and Tony do the argument version by use of a quick cut from one scene to the next.
Christine: Have you ever lost an hour of sleep in your life?!
Tony: I'd be prepared to lose a few with you.

tropes.name: Small Role, Big Impact
tropes.html: Yinsen. He only appeared for a small part of this movie and made a brief cameo in Iron Man 3. He shares almost as much responsibility for the creation of Iron Man (and by extension the entire MCU) as Tony himself — not only by keeping Tony alive, but by driving him to become a better person.

tropes.name: South Asian Terrorists
tropes.html: The Ten Rings, who are based in Afghanistan.

tropes.name: Spanner in the Works
tropes.html: Agent Coulson. The meeting that Tony absentmindedly arranges at a party and promptly forgets about positions the government agent at the right time to save Pepper from the Big Bad and gives her backup at a crucial time.

tropes.name: Stacked Characters Poster
tropes.html: The poster has all the major players stacked on one another.

tropes.name: Stealth Insult
tropes.html:
Pepper delivers one during her exchange with Stark's one-night stand, reporter Christine Everhart.
Christine: After all these years, Tony still has you picking up the dry-cleaning.
Pepper: I do anything and everything Mr. Stark requires. Including, occasionally, [gestures for the bedroom door] taking out the trash. Will that be all?

tropes.name: Suit Up of Destiny
tropes.html: Done three times. First with the Mark I armor cobbled together in the Afghan cave, next with Mark II which is taken for its first test flight, and finally the Mark III with the iconic red and gold coloring.

tropes.name: Suspiciously Specific Denial
tropes.html: It's one thing to question the official story, and another to insinuate that Tony's some kind of superhero. Oh, you didn't? Whoops.

tropes.name: Tanks for Nothing
tropes.html: A Downplayed example. An enemy tank does succeed in knocking Iron Man out of the sky with a shell and he is shown emerging from his impact crater with blast marks on his scuffed up armor. However, Iron Man easily avoids the tank's next volley and launches his own mini-missile at it. He then turns away from the tank to begin his Unflinching Walk as the tank explodes.

tropes.name: Taught by Experience
tropes.html: Stark overrides Jarvis' intention to run a complete diagnostic suite on the new Mark II armor and takes it straight out for a test flight in order get a feel for the new design and whatever flaws it may have. Fortunately, Stark is able to adapt to all the problems he encounters during his flight. By contrast, the Iron Monger, when first donning his armor had no understanding of how to pilot the suit or even shoot straight. With his auto-targeting systems off-line, he can't even hit a human-sized target at six meters with automatic weapons or explosives. The icing problem caught him by surprise, as well.

tropes.name: Technology Porn
tropes.html: The Movie. The lovingly rendered sequences of Tony suiting up are enough to generate a pure unadulterated Nerdgasm. Many other tech-heavy scenes can be enjoyed throughout the film, but these easily take the cake.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: Pepper comments that she expected the Iron Monger suit to be bigger. She didn't realize she was looking at Tony's recovered Mark I suit. When the real Iron Monger appears... oh, how right she was.

tropes.name: Terrorists Without a Cause
tropes.html: We don't really know what the Ten Rings is fighting for. Raza claims it's so he can rule an empire of his own with Stark's weapons, but Iron Man 3 and some of the expanded material have shown that the REAL Mandarin leads the Ten Rings, and that this is simply one chapter of a much larger terrorist organization.

tropes.name: There Is No Kill Like Overkill
tropes.html: The Iron Monger suit worn by Stane at the end is strong enough to literally squash people flat. Yet he seemingly deems it necessary to attempt a point blank headshot with a gatling gun to kill Pepper. In-universe, he's "deeply enjoying the suit", and is trying out all of the "toys" he's had installed.

tropes.name: Throwing Out the Script
tropes.html: At the end of the movie, Tony Stark and S.H.I.E.L.D. had earlier come up with a cover story that Tony was supposed to give at the press conference. After a few questions from a skeptical press, Tony decides to just tell the truth: "I am Iron Man."

tropes.name: Together in Death
tropes.html: Yinsen's ultimate fate, after revealing to Tony that his family is dead, while on his last legs. The two share one last goodbye, with Yinsen telling Tony to leave him be, urging him to stay strong and not waste his life.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Cynic
tropes.html: Despite being imprisoned by terrorists for three months, Tony Stark is still naice and thinks Yinsen's family is alive when he escapes. He is much grizzlier and has no mercy for terrorists after he escapes.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Spoil
tropes.html:
• Paramount marketing put this movie on a heavy trailer rotation for a clean month before the US release, allowing a lot of people to figure out many of the plot elements.
  • Obadiah Stane being the villain isn't made clear until later on in the movie. His lighting and expression on the official poster (see above) is a near giveaway though.

tropes.name: Training Montage
tropes.html: Most of the second act is Tony putting together his armor and learning how it works. And stopping Dummy from dousing him.

tropes.name: Tranquil Fury
tropes.html: While watching a news report on the Ten Rings terrorists causing villagers to flee Gulmira, the home of Yinsen, who sacrificed himself for Tony, the audience can see anger building within him because he knows they are using Stark Industry weapons. During the scene, Tony doesn't say a word but the camera is focused on his face and in his eyes you can see a burning rage growing until he stands and unleashes his first repulsor blast. Realizing that his flight stabilizers can also serve as a weapon, Tony suits up in the Mark III and takes off for Gulmira. When he arrives back in Afghanistan to slaughter them, he continues to remain dead silent, while he shoots, smashes and blows up every single terrorist in sight, liberating the civilian populace. He only speaks three words calmly after grabbing their leader (whom he met when he was first taken by the Ten Rings), disabling him and leaving him at the feet of his would-be victims: "He's all yours."

tropes.name: Travelling at the Speed of Plot
tropes.html: Not a lot of time is spent showing Tony flying halfway across the world to Gulmira after suiting up in the Mark III in Malibu. After a short scene of him engaging super-sonic flight (complete with sonic boom), he is then shown to arrive in Gulmira, just in time to save the civilian about to be shot in front of his son. note  In a deleted scene the need for a transatlantic flight is removed by showing him throwing a party at his home in Dubai, then using fireworks to cover his launch from there.

tropes.name: Treacherous Advisor
tropes.html: Obadiah Stane, a major villain from the comics who drove Tony into alcoholism and took over his company, before Stark sobered up and defeated him, is retooled as having co-founded Stark Industries with Tony's dad, then serves as a mentor to Tony and the second-in-command of his company when the elder Stark dies and Tony inherits the company. Naturally, this being an adaptation, Obadiah turns out to be more villainous than he lets on.

tropes.name: Trespassing to Talk
tropes.html: At the end of the film, Nick Fury breaks into Tony Stark's house to talk to him about the Avenger Initiative.

tropes.name: Twist Ending
tropes.html: Most superhero movies end with the hero's Secret Identity intact, but at the end of the first film, Stark reveals it to the world. This is even after the comic book "bodyguard" explanation is devised as a cover... which is dismissed by both Stark and one of the reporters, remarking on how ridiculous it is.

tropes.name: Unflinching Walk
tropes.html: During his raid on Gulmira, Iron Man fires a mini-missile at a tank then calmly walks away. A few seconds later the missile detonates and takes the tank with it.

tropes.name: Upgrade vs. Prototype Fight
tropes.html: Zig-zagged. The Iron Monger suit is based off the older design of the original Mark I armor, and is larger and cruder than Tony's sleek, new Mark III armor. However, the Iron Monger suit is powered by Tony's newest miniaturized Arc Reactor while Tony is forced to use his less powerful original Mini Arc Reactor.

tropes.name: Viewer-Friendly Interface
tropes.html: The Iron Man suit's HUD is calibrated to appear several inches away from Tony's face to give a good view of the actor while showing the audience how much information Tony has available to him in order to pilot the suit. However, there is so much content (images, charts, summaries, scans, etc) taking up the HUD's real estate in a font size that is readable by the audience, that it's hard to fathom how the clutter would not be obstructing Tony's view and seems to be there to look cool for the viewer instead of being useful.

tropes.name: Villain Has a Point
tropes.html: Up until the third act where he steals Tony's arc reactor and leaves him for dead (not to mention all his subsequent actions), Stane's reasons for his villainy are perfectly understandable. Putting a hit on Tony is extreme, but consider Tony is an Idle Rich playboy who yet gets all the fame and credit for the success of Stark Industries, as well as the fact that upon his return from Afghanistan, Tony suddenly announces he's shutting down the weapons division of Stark Industries, the company's focus for decades, with no plans for what the company is going to do instead, and he keeps a technological breakthrough like the arc reactor secret and for his own private use. No wonder Stane wants to get rid of Tony, he's reckless and damaging to the company Stane helped his father build. (Much of this is subverted by the fact that everything but the fame-and-credit part was a result of Stane's assassination attempt.)

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html: Everything Obadiah does after Pepper steals the evidence of his terrorist dealings and hands them over to S.H.I.E.L.D. including the well-known "Box of scraps" scene. Even his final gambit is nothing more than a desperate, insane bid to drag Tony down with him.

tropes.name: Villainous Valor
tropes.html: During his escape from the cave, Tony shows himself to be an unstoppable killing machine, but the Ten Rings men keep on fighting, and even manage to cripple the Mk I suit, forcing Tony to run away himself.

tropes.name: Weaponized Exhaust
tropes.html:
Tony's repulsor beams started as high powered exhaust emitted by his prototype suit's flight system. Before that, the repulsor was the engine for the new Jericho missile.
Pepper: I thought you said you were done making weapons.
Tony: It isn't. This is a flight stabilizer. It's completely harmless
*BOOM!*
Tony: ...I didn't expect that.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
• When Tony confronts Stane about selling weapons on the black market.
    Obadiah Stane: Who do you think filed the injunction?
  • A smaller one for those who didn't catch it before.
    Agent Coulson: Just call us S.H.I.E.L.D.
  • The ending.
    Tony Stark: [to live audience] Truth is... I am Iron Man.
  • At The Stinger. Famous as the scene is now, at the time it was a truly surprising revelation that this film was merely the first of its kind.
    Nick Fury: I'm here to talk to you about the Avenger Initiative.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html: A variation, as Tony calls Pepper out for walking out now that he wants to protect everyone he's put in danger, whereas before she had no problem with his reaping the benefits of destruction.

tropes.name: When Things Spin, Science Happens
tropes.html: When the outer breastplate is closed during the Mark III suiting-up sequence, the structures surrounding the arc reactor spin counter-clockwise ever so slightly. Justified, as it's the internal mechanisms of the suit helping lock all those pieces it's made out of together.

tropes.name: With Great Power Comes Great Perks
tropes.html: While Tony uses his suit for good and takes responsibility for selling weapons to terrorists, we also see that he loves the sheer joy of flying and being Iron Man. His amazed expression during his first test flight says it all.

tropes.name: Worf Had the Flu
tropes.html: Tony is forced to use his original arc reactor after Stane steals the improved reactor, which isn't powerful enough for his improved suit.

tropes.name: You Have Outlived Your Usefulness
tropes.html:
Stane has Raza and his men killed after getting Tony's first armor suit and its plans.
Raza: I hope you'll repay me with the gift of iron soldiers.
[Stan activates the Sonic Taser, paralyzing Raza]
Stane: [in Urdu] This is the only gift you shall receive.

title: The Mummy
intro: The Mummy is the first film in The Mummy Trilogy. It is a loose remake of the 1932 film of the same name, but as a Two-Fisted Tales Action Horror film with a sense of humour and adventure close to the spirit of the Indiana Jones franchise. It is directed and written by Stephen Sommers, with the story by Sommers, Lloyd Fonvielle and Kevin Jarre. It was released on May 7, 1999. Set circa early 1920s

title: National Treasure
intro: A Disney production from director Jon Turtletaub and producer Jerry Bruckheimer that can be best described as The Da Vinci Code meets Indiana Jones. Ben Gates (Nicolas Cage) is the latest in a long line of the "treasure hunter" Gates family. The family myth is that the Founding Fathers of the United States hid a treasure that was gathered over the course of thousands of years and protected by the

tropes.name: Accent Interest
tropes.html:
Ben notices Abigail's distinct Saxony German accent, but initially mistakes it for Pennsylvania Dutch.
Abigail: I am an American, I just wasn't born here.

tropes.name: Ancient Conspiracy
tropes.html: The questionable existence of the "national treasure" which has been in the possession of numerous historical rulers and individuals over the years including the Founding Fathers. Oh and the Knights Templar actually smuggled this treasure to America where they rebranded themselves as the Freemasons.

tropes.name: Artistic License
tropes.html: Despite what some people would like to complain about, much of the film is a Shown Their Work regarding history (a stark contrast when compared to Jerry Bruckheimer's previous history-based work). There were a few things made up solely for the sake of a plot point to keep the story moving. A lot of the geography, on the other hand…

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
• In general, the idea that the first Crusaders, boots still sticky from slaughtering the population of Jerusalem, would decide to preserve the pagan artifacts found beneath a the Temple Mount instead of e.g., melting them down for coinage is optimistic at best.
  • There were fifty-six signers of the Declaration not fifty-five. Although according to a deleted scene, the clue could have been written before Thomas McKean signed the document, as he may not have signed until 1781.
  • Ben's comment about the Declaration not being in Independence Hall since it had been signed is incorrect, as it was brought back there for its hundredth anniversary. A historian like Ben ought to know that. However, he could be referring to the Assembly Room they were in at the time.
  • George Washington didn't have "campaign buttons", because he didn't publicly campaign either of the times he ran for President; he ran unopposed in both elections, and was unanimously elected by the Electoral College both times.note Since the United States didn't have political parties during most of Washington's tenure as President, he had no need to campaign against a nominee from an opposing party—and almost nobody had any serious desire to run against the hero of the War of Independence. Even if Washington did have serious opposition, the Electoral College voted independently from the people at the time, so popular support was less of a factor in Presidential elections. The office of Vice President was the position that proved to be seriously competitive in the Presidential elections of 1788 and 1792, since Vice Presidents were elected separately from the President in the late 1700s. The buttons framed in Abigail's office in the first movie are actually "inauguration buttons" made to celebrate his two inaugurations.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html: A shot of one of Ian's men on the USS Intrepid looks like he's about to shoot Ben. Instead, he draws a device to generate interference so Shaw can give instructions to Ben without the FBI hearing them.

tropes.name: Bald of Evil
tropes.html: Shaw is bald and Ian's main henchman.

tropes.name: Bat Deduction
tropes.html:
• Ben does a bit of this when following clues. Made painfully obvious by the fact that he's never wrong. He does, however, have the benefit of generations of research into the very mysteries he's trying to solve. It happens enough that he was able to falsify a new clue to get Ian off their back and it was no more or less valid than anything they had done previously.
  • Riley gets quite gleeful when he realizes that he has knowledge and a deduction about the current clue that Ben didn't think of.

tropes.name: Beethoven Was an Alien Spy
tropes.html: The past and present presidents of America, especially the Founding Fathers, were members of the Freemasons and guarded a secret treasure that contained valuable artifacts that have been fought over by numerous aristocrats and other individuals for centuries.

tropes.name: Birds of a Feather
tropes.html: Ben and Abigail both have a passion for history.

tropes.name: Black-Tie Infiltration
tropes.html: Ben Gates sneaks into the National Archives during a gala event to steal the Declaration of Independence which is believed to contain a treasure map to a lost Templar Treasure. Combined with a Janitor Impersonation Infiltration in this case: Ben dresses up as a custodian to get in the service entrance, with a tuxedo on under his coveralls.

tropes.name: The Book Cipher
tropes.html: Referred to by its proper name, the Ottendorf cipher. The various numbers hidden on the back of the Declaration of Independence; these correspond not to a book per se, but to the 'Silence Dogood' letters Ben's father donated to a museum.

tropes.name: Book Safe
tropes.html: Patrick keeps a pair of $100 bills in a copy of Common Sense; Ben and Abigail use the money to buy new clothes to disguise themselves.

tropes.name: Borrowed Biometric Bypass
tropes.html: On their way to steal the Declaration of Independence, Ian and Ben steal the fingerprint access of others. Ben uses Abigail's thumbprint lifted from a glass and placed on a rubber thumb glove. Ian just knocks out a guard and holds his thumb to the scanner.

tropes.name: The Brute
tropes.html: Viktor Shippen for Ian. He's big, quiet, and typically called on to do the heavy lifting, such as smashing a grave open with a hammer.

tropes.name: Camera Spoofing
tropes.html: Riley does this when Ben steals the Declaration of Independence.

tropes.name: The Caper
tropes.html: Some of the loftiest ever devised, from stealing the Declaration Of Independence to kidnapping the President of the United States.

tropes.name: Cassandra Truth
tropes.html: Lampshaded in the scene where Ben and Riley go to Abigail's office to try and warn them about Ian's plan to steal the Declaration—not only does she not believe them (and in fact mocks them) when they explain why Ian wants it, but Riley notes that telling the truth also got all the other government agencies they went to for help to turn them away too.

tropes.name: Chain Pain
tropes.html: Ian's gang throw a chain into a rotating fan to stop it, allowing them to pass through.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Boomerang
tropes.html:
• The meerschaum pipe. Also, "the secret lies with Charlotte."
  • On a smaller scale, the ultraviolet ink on the campaign button.

tropes.name: Clue of Few Words
tropes.html: The first clue that sets the film into motion which Bill Gates sought out to find. "Charlotte. The secret lies with Charlotte." A clue which would eventually lead to the quest to obtain the Declaration of Independence.

tropes.name: Cobweb Jungle
tropes.html: The cast encounters many of these as they get close to finding the treasure, since no one has been there before them for hundreds of years.

tropes.name: Cool Shades
tropes.html: Benjamin Franklin's multi-colored-lensed ocular device. Come on, you gotta admit they look cool.

tropes.name: Currency Conspiracy
tropes.html: To figure out when the shadow of Independence Hall will reveal the next clue to find the Templar Treasure, Ben Gates magnifies the painting of Independence Hall on the back of a $100 bill to read the time on the clock tower. The fact that they do find the next clue at the time depicted (adjusted for Daylight Savings Time) lends further proof that the secret treasure might be real.

tropes.name: Deadly Rotary Fan
tropes.html: Ian's crew encounters a large fan blocking a passageway through the National Archives, but get around it by throwing a chain and jamming the works.

tropes.name: Disney Villain Death
tropes.html: Shaw, when the wooden stairway in the mineshaft crumbles under his weight. It is a Disney movie, after all.

tropes.name: Document MacGuffin
tropes.html: The Declaration of Independence, which has an invisible map written on its back.

tropes.name: Dramatic Irony
tropes.html:
• Ben having to pay $35 for...the real Declaration, thanks to ducking into the souvenir shop to avoid Abigail and the clerk spotting it and thinking he was trying to steal one of the reproductions.
  • When the time comes to read the map on the back of the Declaration with the spectacles, it takes place in the Signing Room at Independence Hall. Lampshaded by Ben himself, with Abigail grinning at the awesomeness of the moment and Riley being his usual Deadpan Snarker self.

tropes.name: Durable Deathtrap
tropes.html: Averted. The mineshaft leading down to the treasure room is a deathtrap specifically because the wooden stairway and elevators the Freemasons built to get down safely have rotted away after two hundred years.

tropes.name: Dying Clue
tropes.html: The entire Gates family treasure hunt started like this, when Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the last signer of the Declaration of Independence, was dying from old age. When he was unable to reach President Jackson, he told his stableboy, Thomas Gates, of the treasure, including "The secret lies with Charlotte", the vessel where the pipe was found.

tropes.name: Eagle-Eye Detection
tropes.html: A necessary skill to find the various clues and advance the plot.

tropes.name: Enemy Mine
tropes.html: After Ian gets away with the Declaration but Ben (with the spectacles) gets caught by the FBI, Abigail realizes they have no choice...so she and Riley go to Ian for help in rescuing Ben in return for the treasure. Thanks to both their being taken hostage and Ben's dad, they all end up having to work together to try and reach the treasure room.

tropes.name: Eye of Providence
tropes.html: The Eye of Providence over an unfinished pyramid, as depicted on the United States $1 dollar bill, is used to represent the Freemasons who founded the US and secretly hid an ancient treasure trove. In the prologue, Ben's grandfather tells their origins dating back to ancient Egypt, and his face fades from view except for one eye over a pyramid missing its upper point, visually evoking the Eye of Providence.

tropes.name: Fakin' MacGuffin
tropes.html: Ben is able to slip the baddies a souvenir Declaration of Independence instead of the real thing.

tropes.name: Family Theme Naming
tropes.html: The Gates family - Benjamin Franklin, Patrick (Henry) and Thomas (Jefferson) Gates are all named after American founding fathers. The credits reveal that Grandpa's real name is John Adams Gates.

tropes.name: Fool's Map
tropes.html: Patrick is convinced the Templar treasure is just a story intended to keep the British going in circles looking for it.

tropes.name: Forensic Accounting
tropes.html: Ben is identified by the FBI because a clerk at the National Archive gift store thought he was trying to shoplift a reproduction of the Declaration rather than, you know, steal the real one. He didn't have enough cash on him to buy it so he used his credit card, which the FBI can track.

tropes.name: Fugitive Arc
tropes.html: Given the litany of minor crimes Ben commits over the course of both movies, this catches up with him when the law gets involved.

tropes.name: Gambit Pileup
tropes.html: Such gambits are pulled by Ben, Ian, and even the FBI ("Someone's gotta go to prison, Ben.") in the course of the film. The last gambit had Ben turning Ian and his Mooks in to cover his own ass.

tropes.name: Genre Blind
tropes.html: Apparently none of our heroes have ever seen an Indiana Jones movie.

tropes.name: Getting the MacGuffin Moved
tropes.html: Ben and Riley get around the National Archives' security by tripping a heat sensor in the Declaration of Independence's display case. The Archives staff moves it into the lower-security preservation room to be serviced, allowing Ben and Riley to break in and grab it.

tropes.name: Good Archaeology, Bad Archaeology
tropes.html: A deliberate contrast is made between Ben Gates going out of his way to solve the Ancient Conspiracy created by the Founding Fathers through the clues they laid out for him, while his rival Ian Howe just wants to smash through all them. This is first played up during Ben's heist of the Declaration of Independence, where his elaborate multi-step plan to get the Declaration out of the National Archives intact is juxtaposed with Ian's plan to go in with his goons guns blazing.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Paragon
tropes.html: The American Founding Fathers and the Freemasons, the ones who realized that the eponymous treasure had to be kept out of the hands of the British or they'd use it against the Revolutionaries, and so hid it away in a place that only someone who found and understood the clues they left behind would be able to find it.

tropes.name: Heist Clash
tropes.html: Ben and Riley steal the Declaration of Independence on the same night Ian and his crew make their own attempt. Ben even lampshades it in the early stages of planning when he notes that the best time for anyone, like him or Ian, would be during the gala.

tropes.name: Held Gaze
tropes.html:
The first variant occurs twice between Ben and Abigail. First, when they are arguing about her coming along with them to keep the Declaration safe: they gaze deeply into each other's eyes and Ben gives in to Abigail, with the Jefferson Memorial in the background. The second time it happens is when the adventurers are down in the tunnel beneath Trinity Church; Ben grabs Abigail, and they look deeply into each other's eyes soulfully before they kiss. Which is then hilariously lampshaded by Powell:
Powell: Why does that never happen to me?
  • You can almost hear the viewer's response in your head. "BECAUSE YOU'RE A BAD GUY!"

tropes.name: Hero Insurance
tropes.html: Addressed and ultimately avoided in both films. In the first, Ian was used as a scapegoat for the Declaration being stolen, mostly due to being an actual criminals in their general actions, including fighting against the FBI. The public doesn't know Ben and family were involved with that part. In the second, the President covered for Ben's actions. Absolutely massive bribes of money and history also helped.

tropes.name: Heroic Bystander
tropes.html: Abigail is chased by one of Ian's Mooks while carrying the Declaration of Independence and hides herself behind a meat counter in a grocery store. While the woman running the counter is initially annoyed ("If you're not a steak, you don't belong here"), she becomes sympathetic when Abigail claims she's hiding from her ex-husband. The employee then tells Abigail to stay as long as she wants, then, when said Mook approaches, intimidates him—despite the fact that he's both short-tempered and clearly carrying a gun—into leaving with nothing more than a few choice words.

tropes.name: Heterosexual Life-Partners
tropes.html: Ben and Riley. It's unclear how they met, but they've clearly known each other for a long time, completely trust each other, and are best friends.

tropes.name: Hollywood Geography
tropes.html: The National Archives does not have a ballroom or any rooms with the size of where they had that reception. The rear entrance where the two are shown are exiting, in fact, has very small rooms where researchers use microfilms and access historic documents. That's not even getting to how Washington D.C. even at night would never have such a lull in traffic along Constitution or Pennsylvania Avenues where a car chase would take place.

tropes.name: Hollywood History
tropes.html: The movie is premised on a (pointedly benign) version of historical conspiracy theories about the Freemasons: many of America's Founding Fathers were indeed Freemasons, but there's no actual evidence that they have any connection to the Knights Templar, let alone that they were able to smuggle a history-spanning treasure out of Europe to the Americas after the order's destruction in 1307.

tropes.name: Hollywood Silencer
tropes.html: All of Ian's men equip their handguns with suppressors that make the stereotypical "thwip".

tropes.name: Imperial Stormtrooper Marksmanship Academy
tropes.html: Every single one of Ian's Mooks. Three shootouts, no casualties. Justified in the first two cases: in one of them, they couldn't shoot without the risk of a gunpowder-hauling ship blowing up, and in the second, the shooter was on target. Ben just blocked the bullets with the Declaration's bulletproof glass shield. The third case took place in a cemetery, and although Ben had cover for the first part of it, at one point one of the mooks outflanks him and misses with several shots from twenty meters or less (but granted, this is pushing the accurate range of the average pistol shot).

tropes.name: Improvised Weapon
tropes.html: When Gates has to get up close with one of Ian's men, he first hits the guy with the Declaration's case before following it up with a punch.

tropes.name: Indy Ploy
tropes.html: While Ben usually plans things out, he's not above making it up as he goes if things go off the rails.

tropes.name: Invisible Writing
tropes.html: A secret message was written on the Declaration of Independence with invisible ink that was revealed with heat. Further clues were embedded in the Declaration of Independence, visible only through a pair of glasses with switchable chromatic filters.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Shaw isn't nice to anyone, as shown when he's asked by a vendor (who is hiding Abigail, thinking Shaw is Abigail's ex-husband) if he wants something. Shaw replies "Shut up." The vendor's remark to Abigail: "I see why you left him."

tropes.name: Keep the Reward
tropes.html: Double subverted. It's mentioned they were offered 10% of the worth of the treasure, but they turned it down. Then it's revealed they accepted 1% of ten billion dollars, which is 100 million. Riley himself got half of 1%, which is 50 million. Enough to buy a Ferrari.

tropes.name: Kick Your Shoes Off and Run
tropes.html: Abigail is kidnapped by the Ian and his crew, and subsequently rescued by Ben and Riley. As soon as she gets ahold of the quiver holding the Declaration of Independence, she surreptitiously slips off her high heels - she's still in her gala dress - and tries to make a run for it, but doesn't get far, as Ben grabs a hold of her.

tropes.name: Landmark of Lore
tropes.html: Landmarks typically serve as backdrop for some of the set pieces. In the first film, Ben explains his plan to burgle the National Archives in the Library of Congress and the ocular device is recovered from Independence Hall. For the second film, Ben, Riley and Abigail find a clue from a desk in Buckingham Palace, Ben kidnaps the President at Mount Vernon, the President’s secret book is stored at the Library of Congress, and the entire third act plays out inside Mount Rushmore.

tropes.name: Let's Split Up, Gang!
tropes.html: When Ben realizes that Ian’s men are waiting for him and his friends outside Independence Hall, he decides to "separate the lock from the key" so to speak, with him taking the ocular device and Riley and Abigail taking the Declaration, and going in opposite directions from Independence Hall, with the intention of making Ian's men split up as well. It works... for a while.

tropes.name: Linked List Clue Methodology
tropes.html: Lampshaded/deconstructed. Ben's Dad points out that there are a lot of clues, and everyone who's tried to follow them ended up wasting their life.

tropes.name: A MacGuffin Full of Money
tropes.html: The treasure. Downplayed as it includes things like scrolls from the Library of Alexandria, which are worth more than just money but everyone still looks for it because it's worth a lot of money.

tropes.name: MacGuffin Title
tropes.html: Both movies.

tropes.name: Making a Spectacle of Yourself
tropes.html: Benjamin Franklin's Ocular Device glasses, not only are they colonial-style, but there are four other lenses, three colored, attached to the frame, all of which can be adjusted to read the hidden messages on the back of the United States' Declaration of Independence.

tropes.name: A Match Made in Stockholm
tropes.html: Ben and Abigail.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html:
• The characters' names are nods to Revolutionary War figures.
  • All the Gates men in the series are named after them. Thomas Gates (middle name unknown, could be any of the five Thomases that signed the Declaration of Independence), Charles Carroll Gates, John Adams Gates, Patrick Henry Gates, and Benjamin Franklin Gates. All of which are justified given the family's links and history. Their family surname could be a nod to General Horatio Gates, who won the Battle of Saratoga.

tropes.name: A Minor Kidroduction
tropes.html: The film opens with Ben searching his grandfather's attic for books on the treasure. When his grandfather finds him, he decides to tell Ben the story of the treasure the family has been searching for more than 100 years.

tropes.name: Myth Prologue
tropes.html: The movie begins with young Ben Gates searching his grandfather's attic for something. His grandfather catches him, but then decides he's old enough to know the truth of their family's secret, a secret entrusted to their ancestor by Charles Carrol, the last signer of the Declaration of Independence. A clue to a treasure from antiquity that had been built up and fought over by kings, pharoahs and emperors, growing larger each time, was rediscovered by knights of the First Crusade, who formed the Knights Templar and the Freemasons. They then spirited the treasure away to the Americas where it was hidden by the American Founding Fathers, with a series of clues and maps to reveal its location, but which have all been lost except the one clue that the Gates family possesses: "The secret lies with Charlotte".

tropes.name: Named After Somebody Famous
tropes.html: The male Gates family members are all named after American Founding Fathers: Ben for Benjamin Franklin, his father Patrick for Patrick Henry, and his grandfather John for President John Adams.

tropes.name: Not So Remote
tropes.html: Ben and Riley are left for dead in the Arctic by Ian, seemingly in the middle of nowhere. But once they're clear of the wreckage, Ben reveals that there's actually an Inuit village about ten miles away where they can catch a ride with a bush pilot.

tropes.name: Nuclear Candle
tropes.html: Generally averted. In the first film in particular, when they find the Templar's treasure, the light from their torches only illuminates the immediate area; it takes the fire burning all of the gunpowder supply line, spread across the entire cavern, to reveal the entire place.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
Ian's henchman Viktor does one of these when he realizes he's about to drive through a construction site, at speed.
Viktor: Oh no.

tropes.name: Peek-a-Boo Corpse
tropes.html: Riley stumbles across one of the frozen corpses of the Charlotte's crew still in his hammock. There's also Mr. Parkington Lane falling out of his coffin, but the circumstances there make his appearance to be expected.

tropes.name: The Plan
tropes.html: This is how Ben operates. He makes a plan and follows through it.

tropes.name: Plot-Triggering Book
tropes.html: The film starts when a young Ben Gates comes across an old tome in his grandfather's attic. After his grandpa discovers him with the book, he tells him the family lore about the treasure that was hidden somewhere in the Thirteen Colonies by the Freemasons among the Founding Fathers during the American Revolution, setting up the rest of the story.

tropes.name: Pop-Star Composer
tropes.html: Trevor Rabin of Yes did the soundtrack for both movies.

tropes.name: Rule of Symbolism
tropes.html: When Ben's grandfather tells him the story of the Templar treasure, the fadeout causes his eye to appear over the top of a broken-off pyramid, thus creating the Freemasons' All-Seeing Eye.

tropes.name: Sassy Black Woman
tropes.html:
One helps Abigail hiding behind a meat counter when she is being chased by Ian's goons.
Meat Counter Lady: If you're not a steak, you don't belong here.
Abigail: I'm just trying to hide from my ex-husband....
Meat Counter Lady: Who, baldy?
Abigail: Yes.
Meat Counter Lady: (leans back slowly with disgust) Honey, stay as loooong as you like.
  • And when he shows up at the counter:
    Meat Counter Lady: [to Shaw] Do you want something?
    Shaw: Shut up.
    Meat Counter Lady: [to Abigail] I see why you left him.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html:
• In comparison to The Da Vinci Code, the film shows a more closer to reality version of both the Knights Templar and the Freemasons. The Templars in question are shown to be more along the lines of an international banking system across the Eastern Mediterranean with the treasure from Solomon's temple being the basis for their money. The Freemasons are also stated to be a successor to the Templars, which is considered fact by members of the Masonic Temple, even including how the Founding Fathers were Freemasons themselves and that members of the Masonic Temple are part of the government to this day.
  • Discussed in the film. Ben's father leads Ian on a wild goose chase to Boston to find a non-existent clue to the treasure's location, referring to both the Beacon of Truth in Solomon's Temple and Paul Revere's midnight ride. Ian never did his research on the midnight ride, so he couldn't double check if the information was correct.

tropes.name: Small Role, Big Impact
tropes.html:
• Ben's grandfather John is only present for one scene in the original film and is dead by the present events, but he explains the legend of the Templar treasure to Ben, setting him on his lifelong quest to find the Treasure.
  • The cashier that catches Ben with the Declaration is single-handedly responsible for both the FBI getting Ben's identity right away and, as a result of Ben and Riley having to change their plans, Ian catching on to them and capturing them in the third act.

tropes.name: Soft Water
tropes.html: Used and lampshaded both at the New York Harbor in the first movie and the Thames River at the second. Justified, since they showed Ben diving the correct way, feet first with arms crossed. There was an earlier mention that Ben is both a Navy veteran and studied underwater archaeology — he would likely have learned how to dive from heights correctly to avoid worse injury. Lampshaded as well when Ian shortly after observes that a fall like that can kill you.

tropes.name: Someone Has to Die
tropes.html: The only way to escape the flooding city is for one person to hold open the drainage door and close it once the rest are though.

tropes.name: Spanner in the Works
tropes.html: Ben doesn't get to use the setup for the Declaration in his home because the cashier in the gift shop he ducks into catches him with it and, thinking he's trying to steal a reproduction, makes him pay with a card. The result is that the FBI is onto Ben from the beginning and Ian gets the clue he needs to catch up to Ben for the rest of the movie.

tropes.name: Steal It to Protect It
tropes.html: Ben and Riley warn both the FBI and Dr. Abigail Chase that Ian plans to steal the Declaration of Indepence but their story is dismissed. This prompts Ben and Riley to steal the Declaration themselves to protect it from Ian.

tropes.name: Stock Aesop
tropes.html: Subverted. Near the end of the film, after being left underground by Ian, Ben and his group find a medium-sized, underground room with nothing in it. They think someone else found and looted the treasure already, and Ben's father tells him that the room is real, the clues leading there were real, so the treasure itself has to be real; in essence, "It's not the destination, it's the journey." Ben accepts that, but points out that the original diggers would have dug another tunnel for air and in case of cave-ins. Scouring the room more closely leads them to the real treasure room.

tropes.name: Sundial Waypoint
tropes.html: One clue requires observing the shadow of a particular landmark at the right time of day to fall on a wall where the next clue was hidden behind a loose brick. While the sun's exact position would change over the course of the year, for the majority of the year it would land upon said wall where the hiding place was. Ben still has to look around for the right brick, though, which is helpfully marked.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html: Ben shakes his wrist in pain after punching out Powell. Wrist injuries are a common result of punching, especially if one isn't used to it.

tropes.name: Theme Naming
tropes.html: Benjamin Franklin Gates, Thomas Jefferson Gates, John Adams Gates, Charles Carroll Gates, Patrick Henry Gates... see a pattern?

tropes.name: Time Zone Troubles
tropes.html: Ben, Riley, and Abigail need to find an 18th-century clue at Independence Hall, which is dependent on where exactly the shadow of its bell tower falls at exactly 2:32 PM. They initially despair when they realize it's past 2:32 and will have to wait another day. However, Riley (of all people) remembers that it's currently daylight savings time, which didn't exist in the 18th century, so they have to look at 3:32 instead.

tropes.name: Token Minority
tropes.html: A nationality variation with Ian's henchman Phil Mc Gregor, who is the only American in Ian's gang.

tropes.name: Treasure Room
tropes.html: They do find one, and it's really big.

tropes.name: True Companions
tropes.html: Abigail, Ben and Riley, by the end of the film.

tropes.name: Unspoken Plan Guarantee
tropes.html: While the beginning of the plan to steal the Declaration is explained (getting it moved to the Preservation Room so it is away from both the crowded public display room and the highly-secure vault), the rest of what Ben and Riley intend is not explained. Unusually, despite this the plan doesn't work out, since a) Ian and his men get in before Ben can escape and b) Abigail, suspicious of him, follows and eventually corners him outside his van (with a detour into the souvenir shop to evade her that gets his real identity revealed to the FBI thanks to the credit card purchase of the "reproduction" Declaration).

tropes.name: Visual Pun
tropes.html: Ben holding up the Declaration's bulletproof case as a shield from Shaw's gunfire. "Hiding behind the Constitution."

tropes.name: Wealthy Ever After
tropes.html: The film's ending.

tropes.name: Xanatos Gambit
tropes.html: The Masons in the Founding Fathers' goal was to protect the hidden treasure. Then their plan to use the Declaration of Independence works to ensure it regardless how the War of Independence comes out. If the Revolutionaries won, then the Declaration would be protected as an important piece of the new nation, and Masons can move it to protect it from thieves. If they lost the war, the Declaration would have been destroyed as it is treasonous material. So the cipher on its back would be destroyed forever. Either way, it protects the treasure's location.

tropes.name: Zillion-Dollar Bill
tropes.html: Used as a joke by Riley, first asking if the pipe is worth a billion dollars, and then if it is worth a million dollars.

title: The Transporter
intro: The Transporter is a 2002 action film starring Jason Statham as Frank Martin: a gruff, ex-military man who is in the "transporting" business. Give him the money, the measurements, and the time and he'll get your stuff from A to B. Frank has a set of rules, one of which includes: "Never open the package". However, whilst transporting a large bag from a somewhat unsavory client, Frank discovers an A

tropes.name: Ambiguously Gay
tropes.html: The director of the second movie has stated that Frank is gay, but it's only written in on the subtext level. Inspector Tarconi's description of his relationship with Frank makes them sound like a gay couple, and Frank turns down the advances of Audrey Billings, but that could just as easily be because she's tipsy, emotionally vulnerable, and married to his employer. (In 3), Frank specifically claims he's not gay, but in circumstances that imply a lie. Though he may just be ace, bi, omni, or pan, and is trying to combat erasure.

tropes.name: Ambiguously Trained
tropes.html: Frank Martin served under an unspecified branch of the British military.

tropes.name: Anti-Hero
tropes.html: Frank is less a righteous force for good and more just a guy trying to get by and keep his head low. This is most emphasized in the first film where he takes jobs from known criminals and only reason comes into conflict with the villains is because they tried to kill him first.

tropes.name: Badass Driver
tropes.html: Frank's main ability but not his only one.

tropes.name: Badass in a Nice Suit
tropes.html: Frank is one of these. He even keeps a freshly dry-cleaned spare suit in his car, for when his usual one gets too messed up.

tropes.name: Blonde, Brunette, Redhead
tropes.html: The love interests of the Statham films qualify. Lai is a brunette, Audrey is blonde and Valentina is a redhead.

tropes.name: Broken Ace
tropes.html: Frank is impossibly good at what he does, as former pararescue (special forces) with a bronze star, but the thing about pararescue is that they drop into situations that have already gone bad and get as many people out as possible. Not everyone, just "as many". He's seen a lot of bad stuff.

tropes.name: Bullet Dodge
tropes.html: Frank does this even without Matrix-style superpowers! (in 2 when the Russian biowarfare scientist shoots at him in the corridor).

tropes.name: Card-Carrying Villain
tropes.html: Half the villains border on this. It's part of the fun.

tropes.name: Car Chase
tropes.html: What the movies are famous for and provide some of the best in modern filmmaking for.

tropes.name: Car Fu
tropes.html: Taken to ridiculous levels. He jumps on a ramp, makes a barrel roll so he could have the bomb under his car snatched by a crane's hook.

tropes.name: Clothing Combat
tropes.html: Frank uses his jacket as weapons in 1 and 3.

tropes.name: The Coats Are Off
tropes.html: Frank carefully takes off his jacket, folds it, and puts it on the hood of his car (declaring that he'd just had it dry-cleaned), before proceeding to wipe the floor with the teenagers who tried to steal his car. In 3 he uses his coat, tie, and shirt as Improvised Weapons during the garage fight. Fanservice ensues.

tropes.name: Covers Always Lie
tropes.html:
Many of the posters have Frank jump to the side like Max Payne with two hand guns, which never happens in film
  • Lampshaded by a trivia section in IMDB: Valentina holds two guns in the third film's poster, but doesn't kill anyone.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html: If Frank ever displays a sense of humor, he's this. Just look at who he's played by.

tropes.name: Determinator
tropes.html: Frank. Doesn't. Stop.

tropes.name: Doesn't Like Guns
tropes.html: Well, more like "Doesn't need guns". Most of the time. All the mooks, for some reason, only attack Frank in hand-to-hand combat, and whenever they decide to use weapons, Frank will conveniently get his hands on a weapon or run away.

tropes.name: Dull Surprise
tropes.html: Frank Martin has two basic moods: beating people up while scowling, and driving really fast while scowling. Sometimes, for variety, he does it with his shirt off.

tropes.name: Everyone Has Standards
tropes.html: Tarconi's a cop, but he respects that Frank keeps it clean. No civilians get hurt? That means only bad guys get hurt.

tropes.name: Equal-Opportunity Evil
tropes.html: The various gangs and drug cartels seem very willing to hire people from all sorts of backgrounds.

tropes.name: Fanservice
tropes.html:
• Shu Qi in the first film.
  • Amber Valletta in the second film.
  • Natalya Rudakova plus Statham himself in the third.
  • Three beautiful Femme Fatales in the fourth.
  • There's also the Zettai Ryouiki girl who tries carjacking Frank in the opening of 2. And my God — Lola!
  • And the female fans get Frank's Shirtless Scenes. Somewhat lampshaded in the third film, where Valentina gets turned on by Frank getting shirtless in the mechanic shop fight and pointing out later that women also like stripping.

tropes.name: Friend on the Force
tropes.html: Inspector Tarconi

tropes.name: Genius Bruiser
tropes.html: Frank is extremely well-versed in the technical aspects of his work, knowing the exact weight he can take in his car and what effects it has on his driving as well as knowing how to use every aspect of the road to his advantage, and has a keen tactical awareness that allows him to plan ahead and make his getaways. That's in addition to being a ridiculously tough and capable fighter.

tropes.name: Giant Mook
tropes.html:
One appears in the first three movies:
  • Downplayed in the first film: One of the villains is an enormous guy complete with Beard of Evil, but is only mildly harder for Frank to defeat than the others.
  • The second movie has a Scary Black Man who's probably the hardest opponent Frank has to contend with.
  • Lampshaded in the third movie.
    Frank Martin: Let me guess. You're the smart one.
    Enormous thug: No. I am the big one.
    [Punches Frank across the room, through a cinder block wall]

tropes.name: Girl of the Week
tropes.html: Lai Kwai from the first film, Audrey Billings in the second, Valentina Tomilenko in the third and Anna in the fourth one.

tropes.name: Good Is Not Nice
tropes.html: Frank doesn't like killing people and he'll always end up doing the right thing, but he's a Broken Ace with a lot of trauma.

tropes.name: Guns Akimbo
tropes.html: As noted above, Lola. While the film posters (like the one pictured above) like to portray Frank doing this, he never does so in the films proper.

tropes.name: Hidden Badass
tropes.html: No one seems to expect a simple smuggler to be a deadly former Special Forces operative.

tropes.name: Improvised Weapon User
tropes.html:
Light fixtures, fire hoses, bicycle pedals, sweaters, motor oil — the list goes on and on. One could call Frank the MacGyver of beating people up.
  • Or the British Jackie Chan in movies made specifically to cater to the American market.

tropes.name: Jerk with a Heart of Gold
tropes.html: Frank keeps trying to be a cold monster. He just keeps saving people.

tropes.name: Just a Stupid Accent
tropes.html: Frank is obviously British, being played by the Stath and all, but he was apparently in the U.S. Special Forces.

tropes.name: Knight in Sour Armor
tropes.html: Frank was pararescue, his job was to save people. That's what he ends up doing in every movie, but he's not a happy man.

tropes.name: Left the Background Music On
tropes.html: Often happens in the film.

tropes.name: MacGuffin Escort Mission
tropes.html: Franks's job and the underlying plot of the movies.

tropes.name: Obviously Evil
tropes.html:
Several examples. Let's see:
  • Wall Street: A ridiculously hammy Sissy Villain in a dark suit with a Beard of Evil, a Porn Stache, and an ever present smirk, who does everything but feel Frank up during their first encounter. He even does a Kubrick Stare on his driver's license.
  • Lola: A Stripperiffic blonde with smeared mascara, who totes a couple of SMGs, looks perpetually high on drugs, and wears hooker boots and a trenchcoat. Yeah, she can't be good news.
  • Chillini: A situational example-he's an Italian man in a white suit in a movie where the villains are drug dealers. Yep, he's a villain.
  • Kasarov and his Big Bad Ensemble are a bunch of sinister Russian Mafiya types who are always looking high on cocaine, Straw Misogynist types, and oozing menace.

tropes.name: One-Man Army
tropes.html: If Frank was in the Special Forces before this comparatively easy job, it sends shivers down one's Goddamn spine of just what the hell he had to fight in the actual battlefields of the Transporter universe. Or the very concept that entire squads of warriors who are of Frank Martin's caliber exist in the Transporter universe....

tropes.name: Painful Adhesive Removal
tropes.html: An implied case. After spending a sizable portion of the early portions of the movie Bound and Gagged, the first thing Lai does once Frank finally cuts loose the ropes binding her while she's at his house is to rip off the duct tape that had been used to gag her. From there, she has just enough time to briefly ask Frank where he's going before she winces, makes a silent 'ow', and places her hand over her mouth to indicate that the removal of her tape gag was fairly painful.

tropes.name: Police Are Useless
tropes.html: With the exception of Tarconi, the cops in the Transporterverse are not terribly intelligent.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html:
• In The Transporter, we are treated to many loving shots of Frank's BMW — up to two of the characters (Frank and Tarconi) telling us exactly what model it is.
  • In Transporter 2 and Transporter 3, it's an Audi.
  • All the Oranginas Frank drank in the first film.

tropes.name: Rule of Cool
tropes.html: All of the movies survive on this but the sequels especially.

tropes.name: The Stoic
tropes.html: Inspector Tarconi suggests Frank is turning into this in the third film.

tropes.name: Technical Pacifist
tropes.html: Frank will kill, but he avoids it. In his opening rampage he delivers a lot of leg wounds and only kills one person, with a Boom, Headshot! as the guy has a gun on him. Faced with another goon with a MAC-10? He takes the gun and unloads into the walls and ceiling. For the rest of the film, the only other person he kills is Wall Street; Lai's the one who kills her father. For all of the ultra-violence in the movie, he racks up a kill count of two.

tropes.name: Tragic Flaw
tropes.html: Frank's not good at being a villain. His compassion keeps getting him into trouble.

tropes.name: Underestimating Badassery
tropes.html: A lot of the villains do this to Frank, with predictably (and awesomely) unfortunate results.

tropes.name: World of Ham
tropes.html: Villains AND Heroes too!!

tropes.name: Abusive Parents
tropes.html: Lai's dad takes this to new levels, what with apparently trying to sell his daughter into slavery. Though he does hold back tears when he believes his last remaining minion shot her per his orders.

tropes.name: Agent Peacock
tropes.html: Wall Street is flamboyant and bizarre, as well as terrifying.

tropes.name: All There in the Manual
tropes.html: Wall Street's real name is Darren Bettencourt.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: Can a set of bicycle pedals strapped to your feet actually allow good footing on a oily/greasy floor? Not really.

tropes.name: Badass in a Nice Suit
tropes.html: Wallstreet is one of these.

tropes.name: Badass in Distress
tropes.html: Lai is a subtle example; she gets herself into Frank's car despite being Bound and Gagged to a swivel chair, manipulates the situation so he's compelled to help her, then shoots dead the man holding her prisoner in time to save Frank from being killed by her father, whom she also kills.

tropes.name: Bad Boss
tropes.html: The 4 bank robbers at the beginning of the film are quietly reminded by the Transporter that the conditions to using his car as a getaway car is that there is to be 3 bank robbers due to their weight, which with an added body would counter the shock absorbers he has installed. So, one of the bank robbers shoots another in the head and tosses him out the door. And for added effect reiterates the deal in a desperate manner. They get caught anyway, but only some time after Frank has successfully evaded the police and delivered them to their drop-off point.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Gunshot
tropes.html: In the ending fight, Mr Kwai holds Frank at gunpoint and marches the latter to the edge of a cliff. As Mr. Kwai is about to shoot Frank, a shot is fired. Only to reveal that it's Mr Kwai's daughter, Lai, who shot her own father.

tropes.name: Beard of Evil
tropes.html: Wall Street and one of his thugs (the sort-of Giant Mook) in the first movie.

tropes.name: Big Bad Duumvirate
tropes.html: Wall Street and Lai's father are the heads of the human trafficking organization, although the film never establishes if they're equal partners or the former The Dragon to the latter.

tropes.name: Blatant Lies
tropes.html:
It is subtly implied that Tarconi knows that Frank is actually involved in every thing he interrogates him about, but always chooses to play dumb.
Tarconi: Monsieur Frank... people wiz zis kind of firepowair don't make mistakes on who they target.

Tarconi: Monsieur Frank. You've always been very discreet in your work, and I respect that. These people. Are not discreet.

tropes.name: Blood Knight
tropes.html: Wall Street, who tells Frank to "keep alive" so they can finish their fight.

tropes.name: Bound and Gagged
tropes.html: Lai, the 'package'.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: The bank robbers offer Frank more money to take them the rest of the way. Frank refuses because it breaks Rule #1. Later he's watching a news report which shows the robbers were caught after driving the wrong way down a one-way street.

tropes.name: Combat in a Car
tropes.html: The climatic chase begins with Frank intercepting Wall Street's Human Trafficking convoy, where Frank forced an entry into one of the trucks via parachute and flings the driver out. Wall Street managed to enter the same vehicle and grapple with Frank a bit for the steering, causing the vehicle to sway a bit while they fight; after a brief struggle Frank throws Wall Street below the wheels.

tropes.name: Cool Car
tropes.html: The BMW 7-series Frank drives in this film was a real life one-of-a-kind vehicle, with the entire powertrain and drivetrain having been replaced to give it souped up performance and manual transmission.

tropes.name: Corrupt Corporate Executive
tropes.html: Lai's dad is a gangster and a "well-respected member of the business community". His partner appears to be one as well.

tropes.name: Crazy-Prepared
tropes.html: Frank has SCUBA gear stashed in the well under his house. Why? Because.

tropes.name: Curse Cut Short
tropes.html:
To be honest, who wouldn't have that reaction when they look through a front door spyhole to see Jason Statham taking a run-up to kick the thing down?
Wall Street's Henchman: What the fu-..?

tropes.name: Death Glare
tropes.html: Frank delivers an epic one after Wall Street's bomb blows up his car.

tropes.name: Defiant to the End
tropes.html: Frank, even when staring down Lai's father's gun plainly states he'd "rather see it coming" before turning around to get shot in the back. His would-be killer obliges. Though it turns out Lai shot first and saved Frank.

tropes.name: Dive Under the Explosion
tropes.html: Frank Martin grabs a Giant Mook and jumps into the water with him to avoid an explosion, using the man's lungs for extra air while doing so.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Downplayed. Mr. Kwai is ready to have his own daughter killed by the end, but it's a last resort and he truly does seem regretful at having to do so. Before this he fully expected that he would be able to raise Daddy's Little Villain, when the truth is Lai hates him.

tropes.name: The Dragon
tropes.html: Wall Street of all people turns out to be The Dragon to Lai's father in the first movie. Points to anyone who saw that coming.

tropes.name: Driving into a Truck
tropes.html: In the opening sequence, Martin drives off a bridge onto a moving car carrier, landing on a conveniently empty spot, then knocks off the car behind him and backs back off the truck.

tropes.name: Every Car Is a Pinto
tropes.html:
• A stationary car is T-boned by a car that's braking heavily and traveling slowly. Both violently explode into flames!
  • And again, when two of the Big Bad's cars run into each other in the finale, and explode for no real reason.
  • Averted by Frank's own car exploding. The briefcase bomb really was that powerful.

tropes.name: Faking the Dead
tropes.html: After the bad guys blow up his house, Frank tells Lai that the pair of them should just vanish and make whoever's after them think they're dead, rather than look for trouble by hunting them down. Lai unfortunately has her own agenda.

tropes.name: Getaway Driver
tropes.html: Frank in the opening scene.

tropes.name: Guile Heroine
tropes.html:
Lai tells Frank that she has to save her family, who are refugees being held in a shipping container. Aware that she's not telling the full truth, Frank isn't impressed.
Frank: You're very good.
Lai: What do you mean?
Frank: The moment you saw those pictures in the house you were setting me up to get involved in all this. Breakfast, giving the excuse to the cop to help me, one lie after another.
Lai: Not everything is a lie.
Frank: Name one thing that isn't.
Lai: What happened in the house, between us. That-was-not a lie.

tropes.name: He Knows Too Much
tropes.html: Once Frank confirms he did in fact "open the package", Wall Street takes it in stride in a joking way, right before offering him another job to transport a briefcase bomb with the intent of dealing with him. The only victims of which were the two unlucky cops still in the car.

tropes.name: Hero Stole My Bike
tropes.html: After the bus station fight, Frank has to steal a shitty car. A few miles and a few hundred miles per hour later, it throws a rod and strands Frank in the countryside and he steals a plane at gunpoint, then jumps out of it and parachutes onto a semi. Then a few cars blow up. Because Transporter.

tropes.name: Hidden Badass
tropes.html: Nobody, including Frank, realized Wall Street was the muscle in the enemy gang.

tropes.name: Human Shield
tropes.html: In the first movie after he's arrested Frank gets out of the police station this way, with the help of his detective friend who plays the hostage.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: Frank broke the rules; he opened the package. Wall Street didn't know that, so that was a post hoc excuse for why he tried to murder Frank, but Frank broke the rules.

tropes.name: Improbable Weapon User
tropes.html: Frank uses bicycle pedals to enhance his kicks.

tropes.name: Innocent Bystander
tropes.html: A couple of highway cops stop to check out Frank's abandoned car while he's tracking Lai taking a wee. Frank has to beat the shit out of them and stuff them in his trunk. Then Wall Street incidentally blows them up trying to kill Frank.

tropes.name: Kick the Dog
tropes.html: The Dragon spends most of his screen time kicking dogs in one form or another, starting with murdering one of his men on the off chance that they might talk. And then there's his speech to Frank and Lai in which he calls the latter a lying whore, accuses Frank of being dumb enough to let her trick him, and finishes with the following line about the 400 people they came to save from being smuggled in: "Just for the record, there were 400 people in that container. Only three hundred ninety-five made it here alive."

tropes.name: Kidnapper's KFC
tropes.html: Once he figures out his "package" is human cargo, Frank buys her an Orangina at a highway convenience store halfway to his destination.

tropes.name: Man of Wealth and Taste
tropes.html: Wall Street, Mr. Kwai, Chillini (who is also a Villain in a White Suit).

tropes.name: A Match Made in Stockholm
tropes.html: Frank and Lai. He delivers her to the bad guys in a bag (letting her out at one point, causing her to nearly escape), and goes back to dole out some revenge when they try to blow him up with his car for breaking the agreement. Frank takes Lai with him (while she's bound) after she snuck into his getaway car. She repays him with sexual favors for this, and also to get him to dismantle her father's human transportation operation. Since he's also responsible for rescuing her, it kinda blends with Rescue Romance. However it's also suggested that Lai is manipulating the situation for her own goals.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: Wall Street: "I tell you, Lai's the perfect name for her."

tropes.name: Mud Wrestling
tropes.html: The Oil Fight.

tropes.name: Nice Job Fixing It, Villain!
tropes.html: Frank was content to simply complete his business with Wall Street and put Lai out of sight and mind. Had Wall Street not tried to kill Frank under the guise of offering him another job, he never would have incurred the transporter's wrath. Frank even says he is ambivalent about whether or not he wants to further deal with Wall Street until the latter's second attempt on his life.

tropes.name: Offscreen Teleportation
tropes.html: Happens often particularly with Wall Street, his gangs of henchmen and Lai's dad, who all seem to be able to outrun speeding vehicles.

tropes.name: Out-of-Character Alert
tropes.html: Although Wall Street has never met Frank before, he realizes when Frank pockets the payment without checking it that he's opened the package (and therefore wants to get her off his hands ASAP) even before Frank openly admits to it.

tropes.name: Punk in the Trunk
tropes.html: Lai, then two cops (both killed when the bomb went off) and for Rule of Three Tarconi after Frank 'escaped' from the police station.

tropes.name: Sexophone
tropes.html: Frank and Lai don SCUBA gear and swim from his destroyed house to another house. There's music. He doffs his shirt. She doffs everything but her panties. She's "making up for the trouble". Frank gives in.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Frank pulls a series of kicks in all directions against multiple Mooks on all sides, resembling a famous Bruce Lee maneuver from Fist of Fury.

tropes.name: Sissy Villain
tropes.html: Wall Street, with his exaggerated gestures, and feeling up of Frank.<!--* SmugSnake: Wall Street-->

tropes.name: Slavery Is a Special Kind of Evil
tropes.html: Frank's policy is one where he works for anyone with no questions asked. Until he finds out his client is into human trafficking.

tropes.name: Switch to English
tropes.html: The Chinese father tells his daughter to converse in English with him (even though she speaks perfect Chinese), because language school was expensive.

tropes.name: Tastes Like Friendship
tropes.html: Frank only opens the 'package' to give a Bound and Gagged Lai something to drink. Later after he reluctantly rescues her, Frank unties her bonds and leaves Lai a microwave meal of noodles, then goes to sleep, making it clear she's free to leave. He's surprised when she's still there to cook breakfast for him the next day. Later Frank calls Lai on trying to manipulate him via this trope.

tropes.name: There Is No Kill Like Overkill
tropes.html: What do you do to assassinate someone like Frank Martin? You have his house shot with several thousand rounds of machine gun ammo and multiple friggin' missiles.

tropes.name: Underestimating Badassery
tropes.html: The bad guys do it to Frank. He does it to Wall Street.

tropes.name: Villain Has a Point
tropes.html: When Frank confronts Wall Street on why he tried to have him killed, Wall Street points out that Frank broke all of his own rules per his own admission. If he hadn't opened the package and just done his job, none of this would have happened. Problem is, Wall Street didn't know that; he's just a murderous prick.

tropes.name: Villainous Valor
tropes.html: Both Wall Street and Lai's father display absolutely no fear when staring down the barrel of Frank and Lai's guns.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html:
An Elite Mook from the first movie had a distinctive tattoo around his eye, carried a whip and took down Frank in one move. Frank wakes up much later, but what happened to the cool mook?
  • A better example is the second truck. Watch the convoy at the end closely: There are two semi trucks full of prisoners, but only one gets "rescued". Where did the other one go?
    • Stopped off-screen.
  • Averted with the two cops Frank beat up and locked in his trunk. They get blown up and Inspector Tarconi notes, sadly, that the investigators are trying to separate their remains from the rest of Frank's car.

tropes.name: Why Don't You Just Shoot Him?
tropes.html: Wall Street has Frank beaten, has back-up right around the corner, and then leaves to let his mooks finish the job, instructing them to keep Frank alive. Didn't the trail of bodies this person left convince you to maybe just finish the job yourself? After all, you were the only one who even gave him a challenge!

tropes.name: Would Hit a Girl
tropes.html: Literally the first shot we get of Wall Street is him abusing a woman. It's one of his women in the pool at his mansion and he has her by the hair.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html:
On several occasions! Most notably how Frank removes the bomb under his car by doing a barrel roll and scraping the bottom of his car with a crane hook.
  • Another example is the climax of the film, where Frank confronts Chillini on board his private jet and the pilot gets shot. Cut to exterior shots of the plane in flight, performing several crazy stunts due to being rocked by the fight within and the pilot's limp body being jostled by the movement. The stunts include a brief moment of flying upside down, several aileron rolls, a tailspin, and finally flying straight up before stalling out and crashing into the ocean.

tropes.name: Ax-Crazy
tropes.html:
Lola.
"Actually, my problem's not medical. (points gun in medical receptionist's face) It's psychological." (shoots)

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html: In the opening of Transporter 2, Frank carves through a gang of carjackers to get to a prior engagement. It looks like another bank job as in the beginning of the first movie only for the doors to open and a horde of schoolkids to run out.

tropes.name: Between My Legs
tropes.html:
Psycho for Hire Lola gives us a good look◊ at her red Combat Stilettos before using Guns Akimbo on the protagonist for the first time.
  • This is also featured on one version◊ of the movie poster and trilogy DVD cover.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Chillini, with Lola as The Dragon.

tropes.name: Bottomless Magazines
tropes.html: Averted when the mooks riddle Frank's car with bullets, then rush to get more ammunition which is locked in the garage. Unfortunately, so is Frank. Lola manages to play it straight and avert this trope in the hospital, where she sprays far more bullets from her pistols than could possibly fit even in those extended magazines, but when she makes her way outside, she does a flashy reload before mowing down some cops.

tropes.name: The Cartel
tropes.html: Chillini's employers.

tropes.name: Continuity Nod
tropes.html: When Tarconi is confronted by government officials at Frank's house in Transporter 2, he uses the same excuse Lai gave him in the first movie: "I'm the cook!"

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html: Frank kills Lola in a brief and rather absurd fight by kicking her onto a spiked wall decoration.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Due to obscene language and bloody violence, this film is considered this and was the first one to received an R rating from the MPAA. And that's in spite of the most common cut of the film featuring several examples of censorship.

tropes.name: Did Not Get the Girl
tropes.html: A little upsetting, but ultimately predicted in 2. She was married.

tropes.name: The Dragon
tropes.html: Lola serves as this to Chillini.

tropes.name: Drop Dead Gorgeous
tropes.html: The film features a ton of sexual tension between Frank and a smug scantily-clad henchwoman named Lola. He eventually kicks her onto a conveniently-placed spiked wall decoration thing and admires her corpse for a few good seconds. There exists an uncensored version of the scene where blood drips over Lola's corpse and the camera moves in to a closeup of her death stare.

tropes.name: Evilutionary Biologist
tropes.html: Chillini is planning to make use of a virus in a decidedly non-nice manner.

tropes.name: Fanservice Extra
tropes.html: The woman on the Jet Ski, with a rapid but generous close-up of her derriére and legs, after being transferred by Martin to the passenger seat on the Jet Ski, in an acrobatic maneuver.

tropes.name: Funny Background Event
tropes.html: Frank hijacks a jetski with a female passenger still on it. They both ride together until Frank lands the jet ski on the road and then climbs up on to the bus after the Russian. When he turns back to look, the woman sheepishly waves goodbye to him.

tropes.name: Gas-Cylinder Rocket
tropes.html: Frank launches one at Lola.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Villain
tropes.html: The Columbian cartels who foot Chillini's bill in the second film.

tropes.name: How Do You Say
tropes.html:
How Do You Say
Gianni: Perhaps I can help you! What part are you a little... how you say, "thick" on?

tropes.name: I Gave My Word
tropes.html:
In 2, Frank has a Rule #4 which is "Never make a promise you can't keep." He promises to protect his young charge; when the boy is kidnapped, the Big Bad informs Frank he's going to have to break that rule. Fat chance.
Jack: Frank, you promised you wouldn't let anybody hurt me! You promised!
Chillini: Never make promises you can't keep, my friend.
Frank: I don't.

tropes.name: Impaled with Extreme Prejudice
tropes.html: Lola is impaled on a wall decoration about ten seconds after engaging Frank.1

tropes.name: Improvised Weapon User
tropes.html: Weapons include coconuts, fire hoses, and an entire boat being renovated which Frank uses to crush a mook after knocking out the support props (the mook was stuck in the porthole).

tropes.name: Kingpin in His Gym
tropes.html: The main villain in the second movie is practicing Kendo against multiple opponents in his introductory scene.

tropes.name: Kiss of Life
tropes.html: Frank steals one from a mook in the second movie.

tropes.name: Mook Chivalry
tropes.html: At one point Frank avoids being shot at by a multitude of mooks, inadvertently averting Bottomless Magazines, forcing them all to grab melee weapons and... Circle around an unarmed Frank, then attack no more than 2 at a time, instead fo rushing him and hacking him to shreds.

tropes.name: Mugging the Monster
tropes.html: Transporter 2 opens with a violent gang of carjackers attempting to steal badass courier Frank Martin's car. When they try to beat him into giving them the code to start the car, Frank opens a can of whoopass that leaves the four men on the ground and their female accomplice fleeing in terror.

tropes.name: Ms. Fanservice
tropes.html: What doesn't Lola cater for? Gun Porn (is dual-wielded, full-auto silenced Glocks with Laser Sights enough for you?), Shameless Fanservice Girl, Excessive Evil Eyeshadow, Intimate Marks on her inner thigh, Combat Stilettos, many a Lingerie Scene (with black garters and Stocking Filler), Sexy Coat Flashing, Hospital Hottie (she's disguised as a medical receptionist), Sexy Soaked Shirt (gets wet in clothes in the fire sprinklers) and Sexy Backless Outfit.

tropes.name: No, You
tropes.html:
We get this exchange from Frank and Gianni:
Frank: Sorry, flight's been cancelled.
Gianni: [sighs] I'm sorry to inform you that you have been cancelled. [draws his pistol at Frank]

tropes.name: Papa Wolf
tropes.html: Transporter 2 is one of the few times you'll ever get to see Jason Statham showing a soft (well, as soft as an unsentimental hardass like Statham can be) and sensitive side; specifically, his kindness towards children.

tropes.name: Psycho for Hire
tropes.html: Lola is a straight example and Chillini is a variant, being an Evilutionary Biologist For Hire.

tropes.name: Revealing Reflection
tropes.html: Frank discovers a bomb has been planted on his Audi when he sees it reflected in a puddle.

tropes.name: Stripperiffic
tropes.html: Lola's "outfit" such as it is.

tropes.name: Tastes Like Friendship
