Philippe is able to clear a path through the babies by shooting out the large hanging lights and causing them to crash down, clearing a path through as the infants leap back to avoid getting hit.

tropes.name: Fake American
tropes.html: In-Universe. Philippe briefly does an American accent which he admits is an impersonation of Elvis Presley.

tropes.name: Female Monster Surprise
tropes.html: Nick is shocked when a pregnancy test reveals that the giant lizard ransacking NYC is about to have babies. Subverted in that everyone keeps referring to Godzilla as a "very unusual he" due to it being asexual.

tropes.name: Finger Wag
tropes.html: Nick does this to the Army during his first face-to-face moment with Godzilla to stop them from firing on the beast while he's(Nick) in Friendly Fire range.

tropes.name: Free Wheel
tropes.html: Used a lot, including at the end when Godzilla is killed. As he falls, he crushes a taxi under him, sending one of the tires flying off and rolling away.

tropes.name: Forgotten Fallen Friend
tropes.html: All the French secret service agents aside from Philipe are rapidly disposed of by the baby Godzillas and the film just as quickly forgets they even existed.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: While the main characters are escaping the Madison Square Garden, there is an intact egg that hasn't hatched yet. This egg survives at the end of the film, and (via Retcon) would become the Godzilla in Godzilla: The Series.

tropes.name: Fragile Speedster
tropes.html: In keeping with the film's more "realistic" take, this version of Godzilla isn't immune to anti-vehicle ordinance or greater, and in the end half a dozen fighter jet missiles are sufficient to fatally wound him. However, he's incredibly fast and agile and able to dodge most of what the military throws at him for most of the film. It's only after he's tangled up in the supports of the Brooklyn Bridge that they can hit him.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Bonus
tropes.html: In the wide-screen version, right when Audrey is in her room crying there's a VHS copy of Independence Day right next to the TV she's watching.

tropes.name: Friend or Foe?
tropes.html: Godzilla causes two other US Navy subs to sink a third sub.

tropes.name: From Bad to Worse
tropes.html: For the crew of the USS Anchorage, certainly. Godzilla swims straight at them, using his dorsal spines to rip open the sub's hull, simultaneously crippling and leaving the sub sinking in the middle of the Hudson River. Seconds later, the torpedoes the sub fired at Godzilla smash into its side, destroying it and killing everyone aboard.

tropes.name: Giant Equals Invincible
tropes.html: Averted, as Godzilla is killed by the Air Force once it's been lured out into the open where it can't hide.

tropes.name: Giant Foot of Stomping
tropes.html:
Used in the early teaser trailer, where Godzilla steps on a museum's T. Rex skeleton in the middle of a kids' tour. Meant as a (typically nineties) wholly unnecessary potshot at Jurassic Park, but really just comes off as kinda Python-esque.
  • Happens in the film when a cab is crushed and later on when Godzilla stomps on a truck filled with stolen goods two looters were using.
  • Subverted with Animal, who is almost crushed but survives because he's standing between where two of Godzilla's toes come down.

tropes.name: Giant Footprint Reveal
tropes.html: The footprint is so large and deep that at first the protagonist doesn't even realize that he's standing in the footprint.

tropes.name: Gigantic Adults, Tiny Babies
tropes.html: Godzilla's offspring are small enough to chase humans inside buildings, hence much smaller than their parent.

tropes.name: Gonna Need More X
tropes.html: O'Neal seeing Godzilla for the first time and says, "We need... bigger guns."

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Done a few times to a few of the Red Shirt French agents when they killed by Godzilla's babies. Outside of maintaining a PG-13 rating, this sort of thing was mandated by Toho, whom are extremely strict about the requirement that Godzilla could not be shown eating people (in this case it was an instance of Loophole Abuse; it's Godzilla's offspring eating people, not Godzilla himself, and we never actually see them doing it), and their requirement of keeping away from "distasteful gore"◊.

tropes.name: Gulliver Tie-Down
tropes.html: Luring Godzilla onto the Brooklyn Bridge gets the creature tangled in the suspension cables.

tropes.name: Handshake Refusal
tropes.html:
• Niko Tatopoulous refuses to shake Mendel Craven's hand after he just sneezed into it.
  • And it happens again in the first episode of Godzilla: The Series.

tropes.name: Hassle-Free Hotwire
tropes.html: Philippe starts a car by just pulling out his knife, flicking out the key barrel, and jamming the knife in its place.

tropes.name: Hate Sink
tropes.html: The titular monster is, as with other examples, a creature that lives by its nature with no concept of good or evil, so there's both the conniving and misogynistic news anchor Charles Caiman, who among other things steals Audrey's story, and the video she took from Nick, and the meddlesome Mayor Ebert, who keeps jerkishly complaining about everything the military does, although he is kind of right to be angry when said military wrecks half of downtown Manhattan on their first confrontation with Godzilla, including blowing both the Chrysler and Flaitiron buildings sky-high, and is focused on his re-election to the point he thinks on his last scene about using Godzilla's death as a publicity booster.

tropes.name: Headphones Equal Isolation
tropes.html: A truck driver at the fish market listening to music and reading a newspaper somehow ignores Godzilla stomping around and causing devastation all around until it chomps on the truck.

tropes.name: Heartbeat Soundtrack
tropes.html: Used to establish that Godzilla really is dead at the end.

tropes.name: Helicopter Flyswatter
tropes.html: With military helicopters.

tropes.name: Humans Are the Real Monsters
tropes.html: The opening titles make it clear that Godzilla's existence can be chalked up to a nuclear test in French Polynesia creating a massive fallout that affected an iguana egg. The buildup and the explosion both show the testing crew showed zero concern for the environment, as trees were cleared en masse or incinerated from the blast. When 'Zilla shows up in New York and causes havoc, it almost feels like karma.

tropes.name: Imperial Stormtrooper Marksmanship Academy
tropes.html: The US Military is profoundly bad at hitting a 200 foot tall, 300 foot long monster. They actually end up causing more Monumental Damage than even Godzilla does!

tropes.name: Ignored Expert
tropes.html: Zigzagged example. Nick discovers through blood testing that Godzilla is pregnant and has arrived in Manhattan to reproduce. He's believed up until his confidential data is leaked (by his ex-fiancee, Audrey), and then his idea is discredited... for some reason. Elsie does convince Colonel Hicks to sweep the city just in case, but by then it's too late: the eggs are real and they're already hatching. If it weren't for Nick and the DGSE already having discovered the nest, this would have turned into an apocalyptically stupid blunder.

tropes.name: I Need a Freaking Drink
tropes.html: Subverted by Roache, who says he could use a coffee instead of alcohol.

tropes.name: In Name Only
tropes.html: Godzilla in this movie bears little resemblance to his Japanese namesake, primarily in regards to his drastic appearance overhaul and being depicted as merely a simple animal rather than a force of destruction. Rather than the camp that is most associated with the series, the script is mostly a Disaster Movie with a bit of action, and the monster movie aspects that remain bear more of a resemblance to The Beast from 20,000 Fathoms than Godzilla.

tropes.name: It Can Think
tropes.html:
• When Godzilla is tailed by three helicopters, he successfully managed to fool them into thinking he is hiding in a skyscraper; cue him bursting from the building behind them and initiating Curb-Stomp Battle. The final helicopter is destroyed when Godzilla crouches low to avoid being seen by it before devouring said helicopter whole.
  • During the battle in the Hudson River, while being attacked by three U.S. Navy submarines, Godzilla swims straight at one of the subs, using the dorsal spines on his back to rip open the sub's hull, leaving it dead in the water and helpless as the torpedoes the Navy fired at him smash into the crippled sub, destroying it.
  • The military manages to lure Godzilla out of hiding in their first attempt to kill him using a huge pile of fish as bait, but they end up bungling it and he's able to escape. They try the same thing again in an area where Godzilla will be more exposed, but Godzilla realizes the trick this time and doesn't walk into range.
  • When the protagonists are fleeing from Godzilla, he moves ahead of them and takes out the bridge.

tropes.name: I Was Never Here
tropes.html: At the end, Animal finds that "someone" has removed the cassette from his camera, and Roche calls Nick from a payphone, saying he and Audrey have the thanks of a grateful France - or they would, if any of this had actually happened, which it didn't.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Charlie Caiman, who propositions Audrey despite being married, and strings her along with hopes of becoming a reporter while making her do all his work.

tropes.name: Karma Houdini
tropes.html:
• Lucy Palotti doesn’t get as much as a dressing down for influencing Audrey to be more aggressive and pushing that Nice Guys Finish Last, causing her to steal the tape and get Nick fired.
  • The French government at large faces no consequences for the events of the movie as their agents cover up and actively destroy evidence in their accidental involvement in Godzilla's creation.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html:
• One of the movie's few truly hilarious moments involves a gag pointing out that the beast should be named "Gojira", but Americans got it wrong.
  • Mayor Ebert at one point angrily shouted to the military's commanders that their choppers did more damage to the city than the monster itself.

tropes.name: Laser-Guided Karma
tropes.html: In a one-off scene, two looters are shown stealing electronics from abandoned shops during the military's first attack on Godzilla. What do know, Godzilla comes barrelling down the street and stomps their truck full of stolen loot flat as a pancake, and just barely misses the two thieves.

tropes.name: Lighter and Softer
tropes.html: Yes, given the original 1954 film was a Genre Deconstruction of the Nuclear Mutant monster films, since it deals very heavy and weighted topics as well as a post-war Japanese tragedy. This film has more humor, action-packed, and overall a goofy summer blockbuster about a giant monster in New York with none of the heavy-weightiness the original film was famous for.

tropes.name: A Lesson Learned Too Well
tropes.html: At the beginning of the film, Audrey grouses that she has not gone any further in her career after becoming Charles Caiman's assistant and she won't become a reporter, to which her friends Animal and Lucy Palotti (primarily Lucy) tells her that Nice Guys Finish Last and she needs to be more aggressive when she sees an opportunity. Of course, that opportunity is Audrey noticing that Nick is part of the task force to get Godzilla, which leads to her impersonating being a reporter (by stealing Caiman's pass) and stealing classified information (the tidbits Nick tells her and a VHS tape recorded by French Intelligence) when Nick leaves her alone in his tent. She makes a report to air on TV, but to her surprise Caiman steals the credit, and this leads to Nick being kicked out of the operation and his theory of Godzilla laying eggs being completely ignored. A couple of scenes later, Audrey is in the Palottis’ apartment, crying her eyes out after Nick calls her out on what she did and Lucy and Animal are arguing on who's to blame for this.

tropes.name: Mama Bear
tropes.html: Godzilla is both a Mama Bear and a Papa Wolf.

tropes.name: Mass "Oh, Crap!"
tropes.html: Everyone in the military command centre as they watch the crippled USS Anchorage about to be destroyed by the torpedoes that the ''Anchorage'' and ''Indiana'' had fired earlier at Godzilla.

tropes.name: Mayor Pain
tropes.html: Mayor Ebert is the "incompetent" flavor. He spends the entire movie whining and complaining about how the military and Godzilla are going to negatively affect his re-election efforts, and tries to capitalize on the event and take credit for Godzilla's death, despite the fact he did basically nothing helpful.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: A "caiman" is a crocodile-like reptile. See Jerkass above. He's also the Butt-Monkey of the film, just like the real life animal. Roache (pronounced "Rowsh") is a sneaky guy who pops up where he's not wanted and engages in shady activities, befitting one military guy's calling him "Roach".

tropes.name: Meeting at Eye Level
tropes.html: After Godzilla emerges through the street and Nick startles him with a camera flash, Godzilla lowers his head to look at Nick on the pavement.

tropes.name: Merchandise-Driven
tropes.html: All the tie-in merchandise was designed and ready for assembly before a screenwriter was even hired.

tropes.name: Militaries Are Useless
tropes.html: The only time the military accomplishes anything is with the 3 F-18s that both destroy Madison Square Gardens and kill Godzilla. Every other time, they fail miserably and either damage or hit other military units. Still, their firepower is established to be a sufficient threat to Godzilla that its primary response is to run the hell away — which is such a marked difference from its normal performance that it irked long-time fans.

tropes.name: Misguided Missile
tropes.html: When the Navy tries to take out Godzilla with subs, Godzilla dodges two of their torpedoes, then swims under the Anchorage, causing the torpedoes to sink it.

tropes.name: Misplaced Wildlife
tropes.html: The prologue shows nuclear testing in French Polynesia interspersed with shots of various lizards that implicitly live on the island chain. The only problem is that none of the shown species are native to French Polynesia.note Marine iguanas are native to the Galapagos, Komodo dragons are native to Indonesia, the Chinese water dragon is native to mainland Southeast Asia, the green iguana is native to Central and South America, and bearded dragons are native to Australia. In fact, French Polynesia has no reptile species, native or otherwise, making Godzilla's origin something of a mystery.

tropes.name: Missed Him by That Much
tropes.html: The Jerkass news anchor twice misses seeing Godzilla walk past the station windows because he's too busy complaining on the phone that he doesn't have a good story to cover. The gag is repeated later, when a soldier mistakes Godzilla's skin for a wall and turns around just in time to miss Godzilla moving out of the way (how he didn't hear Godzilla's growling is less clear).

tropes.name: Monochrome Casting
tropes.html: Downplayed. All the characters with names are white, but some other ethnicities appear as background extras, including the Japanese fisherman who gives Godzilla his name.

tropes.name: Monster Delay
tropes.html: A textbook example. It takes more than forty-five minutes until Godzilla is fully revealed, with the plot gradually building up his appearance, first showing an attack where we only see a glimpse of tail and claws, then his footprints, then another attack where he's hidden underwater, before his largely faceless emergence in Manhattan, and then finally a full clear shot. Even the advertising for the film did all it could to avoid showing too much of Godzilla's design, including billboards which would state Godzilla's measurements and show nothing (which would end up backfiring when Godzilla's redesign took a huge amount of unending criticism, proving it's possible to do this trope wrong).

tropes.name: Monster Is a Mommy
tropes.html: About halfway through the film, Nick finds out Godzilla is parthenogenic and laid eggs. If any one of them gets out, they'll start a new disaster. It turns out one DID survive, setting up the plot of Godzilla: The Series.

tropes.name: Monster Progenitor
tropes.html:
Godzilla is the first of a new species of iguana, fallout from nuclear tests on the French Polynesian islands having irradiated his egg prior to his hatching.
Nick: ''I believe this is a mutated aberration, a hybrid caused by the fallout on these islands. We're looking at a completely incipient creature. The dawn of a new species. The first of its kind."

tropes.name: Monumental Damage
tropes.html: Naturally, it's often NYC's most recognizable landmarks that get trashed, either by Godzilla (the MetLife building, the Brooklyn Bridge) or by the forces pursuing him and his offspring (the Chrysler Building, Madison Square Garden, the Flatiron Building).

tropes.name: More Dakka
tropes.html: The military's entire strategy for killing Godzilla amounts to simply throwing as many armaments, explosives, and bullets at him as they can with no real thought behind it other than that, resulting in a ton of collateral damage and several instances of accidental friendly fire. It's only because of Nick's help that they're even able to find them, never mind hit him.

tropes.name: My Country, Right or Wrong
tropes.html: Roache says he's a patriot, despite the horrible things France has done in the past. There are some pretty damn rose-tinted glasses at play here, though: the US did at least as much nuclear testing as the French in Polynesia!

tropes.name: My God, What Have I Done?
tropes.html: Audrey, after finding that Caiman stole her story and being chewed out by Nick for stealing the tape, is seen crying her eyes out in Animal’s apartment in remorse, leading the two to locate the nest themselves and broadcast the location.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html: Godzilla gets his name from an elderly Japanese fisherman who survived an attack on his fishing ship at the beginning of the film, who is asked what attacked his vessel. He mistakes the creature for 'Gojira', a sea monster from a (fictional) Japanese myth. This is straight from the 1954 original, where the residents of Odo Island believed the creature to be the same 'Gojira' from legend.

tropes.name: National Stereotypes
tropes.html: Frenchman Roche, who complains about weak coffee and eating a doughnut instead of croissants (which are readily available at any store in America).

tropes.name: Never My Fault
tropes.html: Lucy blames Animal for telling Audrey to be "more aggressive" (which got Nick in trouble), even though Lucy was the one who told her.

tropes.name: Never Recycle Your Schemes
tropes.html: Notably averted. The military's first attempt to bait Godzilla out with fish fails because Godzilla slips away between the skyscrapers faster than they can shoot at him, but they try again a second time with the same plan. Only this time, they have far more guns and the fish bait is out in the middle of Central Park, ensuring that he'll be out in the wide open space. Unfortunately, it doesn't work this time because Godzilla learned from his mistake.

tropes.name: Newscaster Cameo
tropes.html: Sports anchor Rob Fukuzaki for Los Angeles' KABC-TV station briefly cameos as an WIDF anchor.

tropes.name: Nice Girl
tropes.html:
• Audrey, upon her introduction, who just wants to be a news reporter. But Lucy tells her that she's too nice to get what she wants, and so she tries to be assertive about getting the story she needed. Well, her attempts at getting her story get stolen by Caiman, and Nick rightfully chews her out for stealing his tape. The rest of the film revolves around proving Nick right and apologizing to him.
  • Despite her claims, Lucy herself is a nice girl when she allowed some homeless people into her and Animal's apartment, because she couldn't just leave them out on the street, especially when a giant mutant iguana is stomping around Manhattan.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html:
• The Mayor was right, the Army did cause more damage than Godzilla did.
  • Audrey got Nick booted from the team and caused the military to dismiss his theory about Godzilla being pregnant.

tropes.name: No Celebrities Were Harmed
tropes.html: Mayor Ebert and his toadie Gene are so much supposed to be a Take That! aimed at Siskel and Ebert that the critics took time in their eventual review to ask why Roland Emmerich didn't go the whole nine yards and kill them.

tropes.name: No Endor Holocaust
tropes.html: It's stated that Godzilla making landfall resulted in "dozens" of deaths, which is quite extraordinary considering we see he apparently leapt straight through a sixty-storey skyscraper. How that didn't kill hundreds of people alone is a mystery.

tropes.name: Non-Malicious Monster
tropes.html: It's emphasized that Godzilla is an animal and not a monster, and at first, all he wants to do is find a safe place to have his (her?) offspring. He doesn't seem to consider humans food, and only fought back in self-defense against attempts to destroy him. The hatchlings only attacked humans because they were hungry and had run low on fish. Subverted later when Godzilla tries to kill four people in revenge for the deaths of his offspring... four people who weren't even responsible, well not directly at any rate.

tropes.name: Novelization
tropes.html: By Stephen Molstad, who collaborated with Dean Devlin and Roland Emmerich on their novelizations for Stargate and Independence Day, as well as writing the ID4 prequel novel Silent Zone and interquel War in the Desert. An audiobook of the novel, read by Doug Savant, who plays Sgt. O'Neal in the film, was also made.

tropes.name: A Nuclear Error
tropes.html: The opening stock footage of a nuclear test isn't French footage but American test footage out of the Bikini Atoll.

tropes.name: Obscured Special Effects
tropes.html: All of Godzilla's scenes take place at night and/or in the rain to cover up the imperfections in the CG textures, resulting an implausibly long torrential downpour over New York that seems to last at least two weeks in-story.

tropes.name: Obstructive Bureaucrat
tropes.html: Mayor Ebert is much too eager to be reopening the city when the military has cause to believe there's still a danger.

tropes.name: Off the Record
tropes.html: After Audrey leaks the tape and Nick is kicked out of the task force to stop Godzilla, she tries to defend what she did when they meet again by saying that Nick never told her to keep it off the records. This only makes Nick more upset and calls her out on her selfishness.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
• Nick initially thinks that Godzilla laid a small number of eggs. Someone then switches on Madison Square Garden's lights, and shit gets real quick...
    Phillipe: (as the rows upon rows of eggs are revealed) Start counting.
  • Shortly after this, one of Roache's men informs him that they have run out of explosives. Roache's reaction:
    Merde!note  French for "Oh shit!"
  • And right after that, the eggs start hatching. And everyone there smells exactly like the fish Godzilla left for his babies' first meal.
  • After Godzilla looks up from the pile of dead baby Godzillas to Nick, Phillipe, Audrey, and Animal and realizes that they are responsible for the deaths of its children.
    Nick: (in obvious pants-crapping terror) He looks angry...
  • During the Hudson River battle, the crew of the submarine USS Anchorage experience this when they realise Godzilla is swimming straight at them with the torpedoes they fired at him close behind.
    USS Anchorage crewman: Sir! The target's coming right at us!

tropes.name: Ominous Crack
tropes.html: The pavement develops a long, spreading crack that runs right under Tatopolous's feet, just before Godzilla busts up out of the sewer tunnels in a shower of rubble.

tropes.name: One-Steve Limit
tropes.html: Downplayed, and also parodied. There is only one Philippe, but one of his subordinates is named Jean-Philippe. The others? Jean-Pierre, Jean-Luc and Jean-Paul!

tropes.name: Percussive Maintenance
tropes.html: Inverted. When trying to get footage of Godzilla, a tape jams in Animal's camera. He tries several times to slam the tape into its slot with his palm, to no avail. When he gently presses on the tape with a single finger, however, it goes in easily.

tropes.name: Place Worse Than Death
tropes.html: As millions of Manhattanites flee to Long Island and New Jersey after Godzilla's first appearance, Caiman makes a throwaway snark about how they seem to expect refuge in those locations.

tropes.name: Platonic Life-Partners
tropes.html: Audrey and Animal have this dynamic, especially when Animal follows Nick to try to talk to him as an act of Big Brother Instinct. This carries over to the series. Justified as Animal is married to Lucy.

tropes.name: Post-Climax Confrontation
tropes.html: Immediately following the basically simultaneous deaths of each of the baby Godzillas within the Madison Square Garden with the famous exception of Godzilla Junior, Godzilla Senior soon reveals himself to actually still be alive after previously faking his very own death down within the Hudson River, and once that reveal happens, the humans soon draw him out onto the Brooklyn Bridge using a damaged taxi cab, where he soon gets trapped within the bridge's suspension cables and subsequently shot down for good with a volley of twelve fighter-jet missiles.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html: As you'd expect for a TriStar/Sony Pictures release, Sony-brand electronics are everywhere. However, it's also Truth in Television for Animal, who carries a Sony-brand camera — Sony is actually a major provider of broadcast equipment, including field equipment for ENG, like the shoulder-mount camera he uses. (Toho's Godzilla movies have coincidentally long featured Sony monitors.)

tropes.name: Ramming Always Works
tropes.html: Godzilla smashes into the Anchorage, slicing open its hull with his spines and crippling it.

tropes.name: Ramp Jump
tropes.html: The taxi runs over one of Godzilla's toes, which serves as a ramp and sends it flying.

tropes.name: Raptor Attack
tropes.html: Godzilla's offspring turns the last half of the film into a fusion between Jurassic Park (1993) and Aliens, with Nick and Philippe's team fighting the baby Godzillas, which look and act very closely to Jurassic Park's velociraptors.

tropes.name: The Remake
tropes.html: Of the Godzilla film series, natch. That said, it's a Broad Strokes remake that borders on In Name Only in many, many parts.

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: While apologizing to Nick for leaking the story, Audrey confessed that the reason she broke up with him when he proposed a few years earlier was because of her job. She was so sure she'd become a full-fledged reporter sooner that she didn't want to settle down. But of course, she got stuck as Caiman's assistant and was too ashamed to come back to Nick as a failure.

tropes.name: Red Shirt
tropes.html: The French secret service agents which accompany Roache. They get little to no character development or focus, and are quickly forgotten after being rapidly disposed of by Godzilla's offspring.

tropes.name: Ripped from the Headlines
tropes.html:
• Godzilla's origins were time-shifted from (implicitly) American nuclear testing during the 1950s to French nuclear testing during the mid-1990s, something which was highly controversial at the time the film was being produced.
  • France deploying secret agents abroad to aggressively destroy evidence of their nuclear tests likewise harkens back to the 1985 Rainbow Warrior Affair.

tropes.name: Rule of Cool
tropes.html: The Apache helicopters featured here have inaccurately portrayed and bizarrely out of place weapons, while neglecting to use several real Apache armaments that would actually be quite handy in such a scenario. Not to mention how they are flown (and the speeds therewith); they're obviously just there for dramatic effect, as it's clear little research was done on them and their standard arms.

tropes.name: Running Gag
tropes.html:
• All Philippe wanted was a decent cup of coffee and on Animal's side, Lucy's gonna kill him.
  • People constantly getting Nick's surname wrong. Even Caiman does this after Audrey leaks Nick's tapes to the news. Only Audrey and Colonel Hicks manage to say it correctly.

tropes.name: Scenery Gorn
tropes.html: Most of New York's streets are utterly trashed by the time Godzilla is brought down, but the MetLife Building in particular is a notable case of this.

tropes.name: Scientist vs. Soldier
tropes.html: Everybody agrees on the fact Godzilla needs to die, but Nick (the scientist), being The Worm Guy, theorizes that Godzilla has left eggs somewhere in the city and thus there should be someone looking for them just in case (among general "we need to know more of the monster to try to kill it more effectively" talking), while Colonel Hicks and everybody else high-up only care about blowing away Godzilla, right now, maintaining maximum confidentiality (even if the devastation Godzilla leaves behind is qualified on its very first day as a worse disaster than the 1993 World Trade Center bombing) and the eggs thing (which turns out to be correct, much to Nick's eventual peril) is a literal afterthought, and when Caiman (thanks to Audrey) releases information that is classified but really is inconsequential, they get pissed that Nick supposedly leaked info and kick him out of "the project"... to kill the giant monster... that is still roaming the city at the very moment they kick him out.

tropes.name: Screen Shake
tropes.html: Nearly every time Godzilla takes a step. Although the earthquakes cause cars to bounce only at the beginning and in a handful of shots afterward, the film still makes sure to make the screen shake with every onscreen footfall.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: Gene finally gives this to Mayor Ebert after having had enough of his incompetence and abuse.

tropes.name: Scully Box
tropes.html: invoked Alluded to but not used. When Charlie Caiman is about to go live with his co-anchor, a woman who has a good six inches on him, he complains about needing something to match her height. He has to settle for hovering above his chair uncomfortably.

tropes.name: Sensor Suspense
tropes.html: Where the submarine is tracking Godzilla approaching them at a high speed.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html: The film ends with the last of Godzilla's eggs hatching. It didn't end up getting a sequel, but the animated series did follow up on it.

tropes.name: Shoot Out the Lock
tropes.html: The protagonists are trying to access the recording booth room in Madison Square Garden, but the door is encryption locked. Animal tries to enter the code, but they're in a rush so he doesn't get it first try. Philippe then just shoots the lock and kicks the door in to open it.

tropes.name: Skewed Priorities
tropes.html:
• Audrey when she steals Nick's tapes; she makes this up to him later though.
  • Mayor Ebert, who insists on allowing the citizens back into the city before Godzilla's death has been confirmed by the military, and at the end tries to exploit the entire crisis as a promotional tool for his campaign.

tropes.name: Slave to PR
tropes.html: Mayor Ebert's primary motivation during the film is getting reelected, moaning and groaning constantly about how Godzilla's attack and the military's presence might negatively affect his image. When he's confronted by a contingent of New York business owners who want to know his plans during this event, he's quick to brush them off, until he's told by his adviser Gene that they're his campaign sponsors.

tropes.name: Slimeball
tropes.html: When Audrey asks her boss Mr. Caiman when she'll be promoted from his assistant to a reporter, Caiman makes it clear the only way she'll get the promotion is if she has an affair with him. Audrey turns him down in disgust.

tropes.name: Slippery Skid
tropes.html: Nick is able to slow down a group of baby Godzillas chasing them by dropping a stack of basketballs and a huge container of gumballs in their way, causing them to slide and crash into each other.

tropes.name: Sole Survivor
tropes.html:
• Only one of the Japanese fishermen survive Godzilla's attack on their trawling ship at the beginning of the film, although based on the way the Geiger counter crackles as one of the French secret agents waves it over him, not for much longer.
  • Philippe is the only one of the French Secret Service agents who survives to the end of the movie, the rest being quickly slaughtered by the Godzilla babies inside Madison Square Garden and then forgotten just as quickly.
  • Godzilla and nearly all of his young are killed by the military, but the film ends with one last egg hatching that was intended to be a Sequel Hook.

tropes.name: Soundtrack Dissonance
tropes.html: The soundtrack features the song "No Shelter" by Rage Against the Machine, doing what they do the best — digs against corporate greed and mindless entertainment distracting from real world issues. ("Godzilla, pure motherfucking filler/To keep your eyes off the real killer.")

tropes.name: Square-Cube Law
tropes.html: Although the filmmakers apparently tried to make Godzilla more realistic in his design, ironically his more dinosaur-like design is far less plausible than the old bulky design. The traditional Godzilla design has pillar-like legs and is built in an upright stance with a low-center of gravity, with massive thighs and thick tail support that you'd expect for an animal weighing thousands of tonnes. This Godzilla has a sleek, raptor-like body held horizontally that basically threw all remaining logic out the window.

tropes.name: Stealthy Colossus
tropes.html: Despite Godzilla being the size of a skyscraper, the military manages to lose track of her. In New York City. This isn't even mentioning how he travelled halfway across the world (including crossing across Panama) without a single person getting a good look at him.

tropes.name: Steel Ear Drums
tropes.html: There's one moment where Godzilla ends up almost nose to nose with Nick, only a couple of feet between them, and Godzilla roars right in Nick's face. With a beast that size, you'd think that the least that would happen would be Nick's eardrums rupturing, but he doesn't even stop to cover his ears.

tropes.name: The Stinger
tropes.html: The end has the hatching of the last egg, leading into the animated series.

tropes.name: Strawman Product
tropes.html: When the '98 American movie came out, some TV stations ran brief reports over the history of the Godzilla franchise to promote it, showing clips from some of the more shoddy Japanese films (such as Godzilla's infamous tail-slide scene from Godzilla vs. Megalon or the ugly-looking monster suits from Son of Godzilla) in an effort to make the new movie's drastic reimagining of the title character more attractive to modern audiences. Essentially, these reports aimed to poke fun at the "old and inferior" Godzilla by deliberately focusing on the lowest points of his "career", contrasting them with the "new and improved" American version.

tropes.name: Strong as They Need to Be
tropes.html: Godzilla's durability and strength varies depending on the needs of the plot. He survives being struck by two heavyweight Mark-48 torpedoes and is only briefly knocked out, but then gets killed by twelve Sidewinder missiles, despite one torpedo having a warhead several times heavier than all twelve Sidewinders put together. He's strong enough to tunnel through concrete, but then can't get into the Park Avenue tunnel, which is right under the pavement. He can run at over 300 mph, except when pursuing a taxi, at which point he can now barely keep pace. His roar can send cars flying, but turns into a moderate breeze when roaring in Nick's face.

tropes.name: Suddenly Shouting
tropes.html:
Mayor Ebert's condemnation of the Army starts as tranquil fury but quickly explodes into this trope.
Mayor Ebert: What the hell's the matter with you people? YOU'VE CAUSED MORE DAMAGE THAN THAT GODDAMN THING DID!

tropes.name: Super-Persistent Predator
tropes.html: The hatchlings pursue humans even when there are still fish lying around waiting to be eaten. Averted with Godzilla itself, as the one behavioral limitation placed on Tristar's version by the trademark-holders was that they couldn't show the Big Guy actually eating anyone: when it does start chasing the cab, it's because it's furious at the destruction of its offspring, not hungry.

tropes.name: Suspiciously Stealthy Predator
tropes.html: Somehow Godzilla's pursuers manage to lose track of a critter the size of an aircraft carrier on the streets of Manhattan. They soon enough discover that it has been using the City's subway systems to burrow around Manhattan Island.

tropes.name: Sympathy for the Devil
tropes.html: Nick looks to be a bit solemn as he watches Godzilla slowly die in front of him. This is explicitly described in the novel, which he narrates.

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html:
• One of the movie's best moments, however, is to its own title; a minor plot point is that the Japanese fishermen who first see the beast call it "Gojira". Footage of this eventually gets out to a certain smarmy reporter, who proceeds to flense it into "Godzilla". Other characters actually call him (or the TV broadcast of him, at least) out on this.
  • The movie's advertising campaign had a quick shot at Jurassic Park (1993), with a major shot of Godzilla's foot going through the ceiling of a museum and stomping a T-Rex statue flat, conveying how much bigger Godzilla is than the prehistoric monster. Behind-the-scenes clips reveal a cut shot that show off the squished skeleton within Godzilla's footprint. In an interview with VFX supervisor Volker Engel, he states that the shot was removed because the skeleton looked far too similar to Jurassic Park's logo.
  • The film was itself (especially their version of the titular monster) has been the subject of several Take Thats in later Kaiju films.
  • One of Charles Caiman's newscasts goes out of its way to mention that Manhattan's Warner Bros.note A chain of Warner Bros. Studio Stores was in operation between 1991 and 2001 and Disney stores have been emptied by looters.

tropes.name: Take That, Critics!
tropes.html:
• In retaliation for giving Stargate and Independence Day negative reviews, director Roland Emmerich had No Celebrities Were Harmed versions of Roger Ebert and Gene Siskel as the Mayor of New York and his aide (respectively). The bizarre thing is, nothing remotely bad happens to either of them (aside from having their city destroyed) and their only real character fault was incompetence (given this is their first monster attack, it's understandable). This particular Take That! backfired on Emmerich, as Gene Siskel said if the filmmakers wanted to get the insulting jab right, they would have had Godzilla eat the Mayor and the aide or squash them (though to be fair, Toho specified that Godzilla wasn't allowed to eat people).
  • Another critic actually is squished in the film: the extra in the car that is stepped on early in the film is intended to be a representation of J.D. Lees, editor of G-Fan Magazine, who had harsh criticism for the film based on information leaks prior to its release. Since hardly anyone in the audience was even going to recognize the reference, it's pretty clear that this statement was just for the benefit of Emmerich himself.

tropes.name: Thundering Footsteps
tropes.html: When Godzilla first makes landfall in Manhattan, his footsteps shake the earth and cause car alarms to go off before he turns around the corner and begins walking down a crowded avenue.

tropes.name: The Tooth Hurts
tropes.html: During the final chase, Nick forces Godzilla to spit the taxi out of its mouth by jamming an exposed electrical cable into the gap between its tooth and gum.

tropes.name: To Serve Man
tropes.html: Despite Toho's specification that Godzilla wasn't allowed to eat people, the baby Godzillas chow down on the French soldiers and Godzilla himself tries to eat the cab that Nick, Audrey, Phillippe, and Animal are fleeing in. Justified in-universe by, respectively, Nick’s noting they smell like the fish (the Zilla species’ food supply) and by Godzilla flying into a psychotic rage after finding its babies dead and trying to kill the ones responsible.

tropes.name: Toxic Friend Influence
tropes.html: Audrey's friend Lucy tells her she's too "nice" and that she needs to be more aggressive in order to get what she wants. Unfortunately, Audrey takes this advice in the worst possible way and steals classified data from Nick to try and further her career (which fails when her slimy boss Charlie Caiman steals the credit), resulting in Nick getting kicked off the operation for the resulting information leak.

tropes.name: Trapped-with-Monster Plot
tropes.html: After Godzilla is apparently killed in the Hudson River, it shifts to Nick and Philippe's search for Godzilla's nest, with Audrey and Animal secretly tailing them, which leads them to inside Madison Square Garden. At this point, they all soon become trapped inside the building as hundreds of raptor-like babies hatch out and start looking for food. More urgently than just escaping, the characters search for a way to contact the military so they can destroy the building before any of the the hatchlings start escaping.

tropes.name: Truly Single Parent
tropes.html: In this movie, Godzilla is parthenogenetic, like some species of reptiles.

tropes.name: Truth in Television
tropes.html: Some lizards (most notably the Komodo dragon) actually are capable of asexual reproduction called parthenogenesis.

tropes.name: Tsundere
tropes.html: A Type A example with Lucy (ironically enough), who henpecks her husband to no end. Near the end of the monster's defeat, she sees Animal in the news and says in a rather loving way, "I'm going to kill him!"

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html: Joe the fisherman who first sees Godzilla arrive from the East River, and flees for his life as Godzilla makes landfall on the dock he's on. He's just a one-shot character, so it's never made clear if in the film he lived or not. In the novelization, Godzilla corners him on the dock, scrutinizes him closely as he begs for his life and leaves him be, badly shaken but otherwise unharmed.

tropes.name: Understatement
tropes.html: "Negative impact" indeed. It's only the freaking Chrysler Building, as Mayor Ebert furiously points out.

tropes.name: Unexplained Recovery
tropes.html: It's never really touched upon how Godzilla managed to stay hidden after getting shot in the Hudson River, but maybe the military is as bad at looking for a 250ft long mutant lizard as they are at aiming for it.

tropes.name: The Unpronounceable
tropes.html: Dr. Niko Tatopoulos, who was named for Patrick Tatopoulos, who worked on special effects for the film and has the same problem.

tropes.name: Vertigo Effect
tropes.html: Used but subtly during Godzilla's entrance in New York for at least one shot.

tropes.name: Within Arm's Reach
tropes.html: In the final taxi chase, Godzilla catches the taxi carrying the main characters in his mouth (as well as a large chunk of the road), but they're able to escape when Nick notices a loose electrical cable dangling next to him which he uses to zap Godzilla's gums. This causes Godzilla to screech in pain, opening his mouth and giving the taxi a chance to drive free.

tropes.name: The Worm Guy
tropes.html: Nick is the Trope Namer, having started out studying mutated earthworms in Chernobyl, but nonetheless ends up invaluable in finding and killing Godzilla despite having very little in common with his field.

tropes.name: Unstoppable Rage
tropes.html: Godzilla flies into a psychotic rage when he finds out all the baby Godzillas have been killed.

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html:
• When Nick, Philippe, Audrey and Animal are trying to make it out Madison Square Garden they get to the lobby only to see it crowded with Baby 'Zillas.
  • When Nick and Philippe discover over 200 eggs inside Madison Square Garden.
  • Godzilla emerging from underneath what’s left of the Garden after being supposedly killed in the Hudson River earlier, much to the main characters’ terror.

tropes.name: Won't Get Fooled Again
tropes.html: The military is able to lure Godzilla out of the subways using a giant pile of fish as bait. They mess it up by placing the bait in a confined area, and Godzilla is able to escape through the winding city streets. They try the same trick again, but place the bait in the middle of Central Park where there will be no cover for Godzilla to hide behind. However, he's not stupid enough to fall for the same thing a second time after seeing it being lit up with spotlights.

tropes.name: Wormsign
tropes.html: When Godzilla arrives from the ocean, the pier splits most satisfyingly.

tropes.name: Writers Cannot Do Math
tropes.html: Echos 1, 2, and 4 all reporting for duty, but no Echo 3?

tropes.name: Your Size May Vary
tropes.html: Godzilla is very inconsistent throughout the film; for example, when he first emerges from the sewer, his eye appears to be roughly a metre in diameter, while in a later scene it seems to completely dwarf an entire person.

tropes.name: Your Tomcat Is Pregnant
tropes.html: Godilla is pregnant despite being the only one of its kind, but is still referred to as "he". note A phenomenon known as parthogenesis, a form of asexual reproduction which does not require males, found in some reptiles.

title: One Hundred and One Dalmatians
intro: Entry #17 in the Disney Animated Canon, The Hundred and One Dalmatians was adapted for animation by Walt Disney Pictures as One Hundred and One Dalmatians.note Usually promoted with the Arabic numeral as 101 Dalmatians. The second Disney animated film to be set unambiguously in contemporary time period,note It is sometimes thought to be the first Disney animated film set in present day, but the fi

tropes.name: Actionized Adaptation
tropes.html: A Disney version — in the book Pongo and Misses never confront the Badduns directly but infiltrate Hell Hall and sneak everyone out through a back exit. There is also no dramatic Car Fu scene between Cruella and the moving van: they simply hunker down in the back and hide their eyes so she doesn't see them. However, the scene in the book where they break into her London home and tear her furs to shreds is completely omitted.

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html:
• Roger and Anita laugh following the Meet Cute scene when Anita tries to wipe herself dry with a handkerchief, only to find it's sodden, and Roger's handkerchief is as well.
  • Pongo enjoys Roger's song and impression of "Cruella de Vil" after she barges in and asks about Perdita's unborn puppies. Anita tries to put on an invoked Dude, Not Funny! front since she's trying to be civil to Cruella but eventually she breaks down giggling offscreen when Roger waltzes with her to the melody.

tropes.name: Adaptational Job Change
tropes.html: In the book Mr. Dearly has an office job; in the film Roger is a struggling songwriter.

tropes.name: Adaptational Ugliness
tropes.html: The original book illustrations show Cruella as being fairly attractive-looking in spite of her cold-blooded personality. The movie, in contrast, makes her very ugly to fit her more eccentric personality in the adaptation. Early designs for her by her animator Marc Davis keep truer to the book's design.

tropes.name: Adaptation Distillation
tropes.html: Both the original author and Disney himself praised the story's streamlining.

tropes.name: Adaptation Name Change
tropes.html: Mr. and Mrs. Dearly were changed to Roger and Anita Radcliffe for the animated movie. Later adaptations give them the given names from the movie and the surname from the book. Also, Saul Badun becomes Horace, Roly Poly becomes simply Rolly, and Lt. Tib becomes Sgt. Tibbs (with that particular cat also getting a sex change in the process).

tropes.name: Adapted Out
tropes.html: A few non-important characters from the novel were removed like Cruella's husband and cat, Cadpig (although she appeared in the animated series), and Perdita's old boyfriend Prince (who was mainly important in the book as dalmatian number 101 and part of an implied Beta Couple.)

tropes.name: Added Alliterative Appeal
tropes.html: During the break-in, Nanny refers to the tall and lanky Jasper as a big Long-Legged Lummox.

tropes.name: Angrish
tropes.html: Roger stutters, yet holds firm, when telling Cruella that he and Anita are not selling their puppies.

tropes.name: Animals Hate Him
tropes.html: Cruella de Vil is hated by the titular dalmatian family and virtually every other animal she comes across. But being the Trope Namer of Cruella to Animals, it's more than justified.

tropes.name: Argument of Contradictions
tropes.html:
When Patch and Lucky push each other in the fireplace, they argue "Did not!" (Lucky) and "Did too!" (Patch) about who did it first.
Lucky: Did not.
Patch: Did too.
Lucky: Did not.
Patch: Did too.
Lucky: Did not! (sticks his tongue out)
Perdita: Please, children, don't quarrel.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Animal Care
tropes.html: The titular puppies, at one point, are fed on cow's milk, straight from the source (in other words, raw milk). Most animals are lactose intolerant, and dogs are no exception. The puppies were probably already past the age at which they could digest milk, so in Real Life it would have given them severe diarrhea and upset stomachs. The fact that they were starving far away from other food sources at least makes drinking or eating something they normally shouldn't the lesser of two evils in this particular case.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Chemistry
tropes.html: To get Jasper's attention, Cruella yanks what appears to be a wine bottle out of his hands while he's drinking it and flings it backhand into the fireplace, where it shatters and then explodes with a loud bang. Wine doesn't have enough alcohol in it to explode even if aerosolized like this.

tropes.name: Artistic Licence – Geography
tropes.html:
An American road sign appears in the British countryside during the climactic car chase.
  • There's a lot of real world spaces in the movie. Dinsford though isn't a real British village in Suffolk.

tropes.name: Badass Bystander
tropes.html: The van driver who has to deal with Cruella ramming him several times in the climax, hoping to first send him in the snow and then off a cliff. He merely yells at her, mutters, "Crazy woman driver," and focuses on keeping the van on the road.

tropes.name: Bad People Abuse Animals
tropes.html: Cruella DeVil is so driven to have a dalmatian fur coat to compliment her fur coat obsession that she orders her goons to break into a house and steal some and then kill them all in the quickest way possible ("Any way you like — poison them, drown them, bash them in the head!").

tropes.name: Bag of Kidnapping
tropes.html: Jasper and Horace put the puppies in the sack.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html:
• At the end of the final chase, Jasper and Horace break their steering wheel and the loss of control causes them to collide with Cruella's car and fall down the hill underneath the bridge, allowing the Dalmatians to escape. What follows is a very grim scene where we see the wrecked remnants of both of their vehicles lying in the snow, and we are about to assume the worst has just happened right before our eyes...only for the camera to suddenly pan to the left, revealing that Cruella, Jasper, and Horace all survived the crash.
  • When Sergeant Tibbs is trying to convince the puppies to escape with him, he hears Horace shout "Look!" and dives for cover, but Horace hadn't spotted him, he was just amused to see someone they knew on the game show he and Jasper were watching.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Comparison
tropes.html: When Cruella DeVil tells Jasper and Horace to kill the Dalmatian puppies, the camera shows a shot of the puppies listening to the conversation as Jasper pleads for her to have pity... before asking "Can't we see the rest of the show first?"

tropes.name: Beauty Is Relative
tropes.html: Pongo admits that dogs are poor judges on human beauty when he was looking for a potential mate for his "pet", Rodger Radcliffe. However, when simply gazing outside, he notices some walking by and does make some accurate judgements on both the humans and their dogs. He naturally becomes completely smitten when first gazing upon Perdita, a female dalmatian, and as before, he accurately judges Anita, Perdita's "pet", as very lovely, too.

tropes.name: "Be Quiet!" Nudge
tropes.html:
Jasper nudges Horace when they try to trick Nanny Cook into letting them inside and take the puppies, by pretending that they're from the electric company.
Jasper: Ah, good evenin', mum. We're here to inspect the wirin' and the switches.
Horace: Uh, we're from the gas company.
Jasper: [whispering] 'Lectric. 'Llectric.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: Cruella seems like a somewhat pleasant woman at first, if a bit snide and condescending, but she really didn't like being told the Radcliffes weren't interested in selling the puppies.

tropes.name: Beware the Nice Ones
tropes.html:
• Roger may be a goofball with No Social Skills, but you don't barge into his flat right after he's saved a stillborn puppy, make several catty remarks about calling the newborns "little white rats," and then have the gall to "buy them all" expecting to get an acceptance.
  • Pongo and Perdita are as charming and adorable as animated dogs can be. As long as you don't mess with their children.

tropes.name: Big Brother Instinct
tropes.html: Patch is technically the same age as his 14 other siblings, but he adopts this attitude towards Lucky and the others. When Horace and Jasper push down Lucky to stop him from hogging the TV, Patch angrily barks at them. He later says that the other 84 puppies need help and protection from Cruella and the Baduns.

tropes.name: Big Damn Heroes
tropes.html: Pongo and Perdita bursting into Hell Hall just in time to stop Horace and Jasper from killing all the puppies.

tropes.name: Big "SHUT UP!"
tropes.html: Cruella yells this at Horace and Jasper a lot. It comes back later as she's having a tantrum over having lost the puppies and ending up in a ditch, much to the irritation of Jasper.

tropes.name: Big "WHAT?!"
tropes.html: While Jasper is on the phone to Cruella, he snaps at Horace, “Shut up, you idiot!” Cruella yells this at him, thinking he said it to her. Jasper quickly clarifies he said it to Horace.

tropes.name: Born During a Storm
tropes.html: Perdita gives birth during a rainy October night. The patter of falling rain and the occasional distant sound of thunder adds to the anxiety of the scene as Roger and Pongo wait outside, then when Roger is reviving one of the puppies. When Cruella bursts in to buy the whole litter, she is backlit by a flash of lightning, accompanied by a loud thunderclap.

tropes.name: Bowdlerize
tropes.html: Promotional stills of the Diamond Edition Blu-Ray release edited out Cruella's cigar and smoke in her shots, although it was left in the film proper with a PSA against smoking added to the trailers on the disc.

tropes.name: Braving the Blizzard
tropes.html: The Dalmatians have to walk through a blizzard at the start of their journey home. It's very tough, and Lucky has to be carried by Pongo, as he's too exhausted and cold to walk.

tropes.name: Butt Biter
tropes.html: During the scene when Pongo and Perdita break into the house to rescue their puppies, they get into a fight with Horace and Jasper. During said fight, Pongo bites Jasper's butt.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Some of the dogs from Lady and the Tramp make cameos during the citywide dog barking scene, including Tramp (on top of a car), Lady (in the street), Jock, and Peg (along with the bulldog from the pound who seems to have had puppies with her).

tropes.name: Canines Primary, Felines Secondary
tropes.html: Sergeant Tibbs, the heroic cat, ranks lower than Colonel, the dog. Also, Tibbs is the lone cat in a movie whose cast is made up mostly of dogs.

tropes.name: Cat Scare
tropes.html: Happens twice. The first time, Tibbs is right next to a bottle of rum; Jasper tries to take a swig from the bottle and mistakenly tries to drink the cat. The second time is when Tibbs is helping the puppies to hide. Tibbs can't take on Horace and Jasper on his own, but when Jasper looks under the bed, the ensuing MEEEOOWWWW and wild leap from Tibbs startles Jasper enough for the puppies to run past him.

tropes.name: Censorship by Spelling
tropes.html: Pongo suggests getting the puppies to bed so he and Perdita can go out on a W-A-L-K. While not explicitly stated whether the puppies know how to spell, a couple of them do beg to stay up and join their parents on the walk.

tropes.name: Ceiling Banger
tropes.html: Nanny does this to get Roger to take a break from writing songs.

tropes.name: Chase Scene
tropes.html: While most of the plot is a chase, the straightest example comes when Cruella chases after the van in which Pongo, Perdita, and the puppies are making their escape.

tropes.name: Cheated Angle
tropes.html: The climax has a peculiar example of this combined with sleight of hand editing. When it starts, Cruella and her lackeys split up in different directions. Later on, Jasper and Horace show up at the top of the hill with a road crossing the same path as the Moving Van, and when the point of view switches to their car, we can see that they're correctly coming towards the left of the moving van the dalmatians hitched a ride on. But in the shots just before Jasper and Horace lose control of their truck and T-Bone Cruella's car, there are two gaffes—first, the van and hill has magically moved to the right side of the van when the camera switches to the Moving Van drivers POV. And as if that wasn't enough, in the Moving Vans POV, we can clearly see Jasper and Horace are almost at the bottom of the hill. But in the next shots, right after they break their steering wheel and go reeling down the bank and into Cruella's car, they somehow magically teleported back up the hill! Given how extensively Disney planned their films, Its more than likely they purposely ignored continuity for the sake of staging and cinematic effect.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html:
• The dogs that Pongo sees strolling on the street before Perdita and Anita appear later reappear to relay the message that the puppies have been stolen.
  • The truck that nearly hits Pongo and Perdita on their journey to Hell Hall is the same truck that will later take them and their puppies back to London.

tropes.name: Christmas Epilogue
tropes.html: Pongo, Perdita, and the puppies are reunited at the Radcliffs' house as they are decorating for Christmas.

tropes.name: Clean Pretty Reliable
tropes.html: One of the 15 (the eventual "Lucky") was apparently stillborn, leading Roger to get an idea, rubbing the pup rapidly to stimulate it to breathe. It does the trick, and Lucky starts moving within the blanket.

tropes.name: Clock Tampering
tropes.html: At the beginning, Pongo forwards the time on Roger's clock so he can go for his 5:00 walk in the park and get Roger and Anita, plus him and Perdita, to meet.

tropes.name: Clothes Make the Legend
tropes.html: One of the most famous fur coats ever. Ironic considering it never actually gets made (which considering the villain's theme, may as well been intentional).

tropes.name: Combat Pragmatist
tropes.html: As fierce as they were against Horace and Jasper, Pongo and Perdita actually dispose of them by barely touching them at all, instead using their lair's surroundings against them or fooling them into hurting themselves in their own buffoonery (most likely to keep their cathartic "mauling" of them G-Rated).

tropes.name: Come Out, Come Out, Wherever You Are
tropes.html: Jasper whistles and says "Here, puppies, come on out" while he and Horace are looking for them in the mansion.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html:
• In the book, four of the Dalmatians are adults: the two main characters are named Pongo and Missis, and the Dearlys round out their numbers with an abandoned dog named Perdita and her long-lost mate. In the film, there are only two adult Dalmatians, named Pongo and Perdita.
  • Nanny Cook and Nanny Butler are merged into a single "Nanny".
  • Cadpig, the delicate puppy who was revived as a newborn, is merged with Lucky, the brave leader.

tropes.name: Conversational Troping
tropes.html: The bit where they watch Thunderbolt's show ("Ol' Thunder always wins!").

tropes.name: Cool Car
tropes.html: Cruella's car. A lot of people have put effort into trying to figure out what model it is, though it most closely resembles a 1936 Alvis Speed 20 Drophead Coupe, similar to this one◊. It's just too bad that Cruella's obsession with making a fur coat out of the dalmatians led her to trash the car...

tropes.name: Crazed Concentric Eyes
tropes.html: Cruella de Vil's eyes are shown with a thin black spiral and tiny asterisks for pupils when she goes on a violent Road Rage at the climax of the film.

tropes.name: Creator's Show Within a Show
tropes.html: Horace and Jasper can be seen watching Silly Symphonies.

tropes.name: Creepy Jazz Music
tropes.html: Roger sings (and plays) a jazzy "The Villain Sucks" Song about Cruella de Vil, which describes how wicked and heartless she is.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html: Horace and Jasper are on the receiving end of this when Pongo and Perdita charge in just as they were about to attack the puppies.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Cushion
tropes.html: Unlike Horace against Perdita which is completely slapstick, Jasper and Pongo's fight does briefly turn vicious, with Jasper managing to kick Pongo hard into the wall, the latter even having an Oh, Crap! moment as Jasper comes at him with his crowbar. Pongo dodges and bites him in the ass for it (dragging his pants down with it), but the crowbar smashing clear through the wall shows that Jasper nearly killed Pongo.

tropes.name: Dangerous Backswing
tropes.html: In one scene, Horace accidentally bonks Jasper in the head with a club.

tropes.name: Dangerous Clifftop Road
tropes.html: Cruella car-chases the truck with the dalmatian puppies along such a dangerous clifftop road.

tropes.name: Dangerous Interrogative
tropes.html:
After Perdita's puppies are born, Cruella shows up with an offer to buy them for herself. She ends up doing this when Roger nervously, but defiantly, declares that the puppies will not be sold.
Cruella: (writing a check) When can the puppies leave their mother? Two weeks? Three weeks?
Roger: Never!
Cruella: (gets up and into Roger's face) What...?
Roger: We-We-We're not... not s-s-selling... th-the puppies. N-Not a single, single one! You understand?

tropes.name: Dartboard of Hate
tropes.html: The movie briefly has Jasper throwing darts at a portrait of the prime minister for some unknown reason.

tropes.name: Death Glare
tropes.html:
• Roger and Pongo both give one to Cruella when she has made fun of Roger's songwriting career. Their expressions didn't seem to change after they were splattered with ink from Cruella's pen.
  • A cut verse from "Cruella De Vill" mentions Cruella's:
    The curl of her lips, the ice in her stare/all innocent children had better beware...

tropes.name: Deus ex Machina
tropes.html: The Dalmatians had nothing to do with their final escape from the villains. It was pure chance that a panicked Horace yanked out the steering wheel of the Baduns' truck, causing them to lose control and T-bone Cruella's car.

tropes.name: Disney Death
tropes.html:
• One of the initial litter of puppies (Lucky, although in the original book it was Cadpig) appears to be dead, but is resuscitated by Roger rubbing him. Yes, a Disney Death moment for a character that's only just been born.
  • This also happens in the Thunderbolt TV show. Patch is Genre Savvy enough to realize that Thunderbolt survived.

tropes.name: Distinguished Gentleman's Pipe
tropes.html: Roger is almost always seen with his trademark pipe in the movie.

tropes.name: The Dog Bites Back
tropes.html:
• Not one of the dogs, but at the end, as the defeated Cruella has her Villainous Breakdown which involves verbally assaulting Horace and Jasper some more, Jasper calmly replies, "Aw, shaddap!"
  • A literal example in the brawl between Pongo against Jasper; after being kicked in the face by the thug, he manages to dodge the poker that Jasper was going to bludgeon his head with before biting him really hard in the bum.

tropes.name: Dogs Are Dumb
tropes.html: Subverted with most of them, but played straight with the Colonel. In the book, the Colonel is much less bumbling and more of an actual military commander, teaching the dogs how to fight and promoting them whenever they do something awesome.

tropes.name: Dog Walks You
tropes.html: Happens with Pongo and Roger in the early parts of the movie, as part of the Meet Cute.

tropes.name: Domestic-Only Cartoon
tropes.html: As with any film of Walt Disney Animation Studios produced during this period. This is also one of only two animated productions of the 101 Dalmatians franchise to be produced as such, the other being the pitch pilot episode of the British-produced 101 Dalmatian Street.

tropes.name: Doomed New Clothes
tropes.html: Anita Radcliff has spent hours ironing her new spring suit, but there she goes into the pond! Note that when you combine Meet Cutes and new clothes the probability of catastrophe increase exponentially.

tropes.name: Door Slam of Rage
tropes.html:
Done twice by Cruella, both times hard enough to result in property damage:
  • When the Radcliffes refuse to sell their puppies to her, she storms out of their flat, slamming the door hard enough to shatter the window panes on it.
  • Later at Hell Hall, after she angrily orders Horace and Jasper to kill the puppies so she can make her coat, she slams the door behind her with enough force to cause a large crack to rise up the wall and across the ceiling, from which a chunk of plaster falls onto Horace's head.

tropes.name: The Door Slams You
tropes.html:
Three times.
  • Early on, when Cruella shows up looking to buy the puppies, she slams poor Nanny. Later, when Horace and Jasper barge in to steal the puppies, they do the same thing.
  • It happens again much later, just before the climactic Chase Scene. Having discovered that the Dalmatians have disguised themselves as black Labradors, Cruella yells for Jasper and Horace while impatiently honking the horn of her car. The Baduns are inside a blacksmith's shed with a large, locked wooden door that leads out to the street. Upon hearing Cruella's yells, they break down the door — which falls right into Cruella's face, as it turns out that she had parked right outside it.

tropes.name: Dope Slap
tropes.html: Ironically, Jasper's usual response to Horace's Dumbass Has a Point moments.

tropes.name: Dramatic Thunder
tropes.html: A loud one rolls right before the 15th puppy gets resurrected.

tropes.name: Dramatic TV Shut-Off
tropes.html:
Near the end, Roger turns off a nearby radio playing his song "Cruella de Vil", not out of anger or embarrassment, but because he's still down over the Dalmatians' disappearance.
Anita: Roger, after all that, your first big hit. It's made more money than we ever dreamed of.
Roger: Yes, I know. But I still can't believe that Pongo and Perdie would run away.

tropes.name: Dreaming of a White Christmas
tropes.html: The movie is set in Britain, and on their way from Suffolk back to London, the puppies go home in the snow and it's said to be around Christmas time.

tropes.name: Drives Like Crazy
tropes.html: Cruella is so obsessed with getting her fur coat, she resorts to road rage which does not fare well for her car.

tropes.name: Dub Name Change
tropes.html: The Finnish dub has Horace's name changed to Jesper.

tropes.name: Dumbass Has a Point
tropes.html: Horace is clearly not the sharpest tool in the shed, but by assuming that dogs think the same way that people think (which is true in this movie), he is constantly suggesting what the dogs are actually doing while trying to evade the Baduns. He's almost always right, but Jasper will have none of it.

tropes.name: Epic Hail
tropes.html: Pongo and Perdita use the "Twilight Bark" as a last ditch effort to locate their missing puppies. To humans, it's just wild, sudden barking that causes other dogs within earshot to follow suit (and remember, dogs have really good hearing).

tropes.name: "Eureka!" Moment
tropes.html: When Pongo sees two of his little ones covered in soot, he gets the idea for the disguise as black Labradors.

tropes.name: Every Car Is a Pinto
tropes.html: Averted. When Horace and Jasper's truck crashes into Cruella's car at the end, both vehicles get smashed to bits as they fly off the edge of a cliff, but there's no explosion.

tropes.name: Evil-Detecting Dog
tropes.html: Just about every dog can tell Cruella is pure evil. Pongo and Perdita can tell straight away, with Perdita fearfully saying, "It's her... it's that devil woman" when Cruella drives up to the Radcliffes' flat the first time, and Pongo growling angrily at Cruella when she beckons him to come over to her.

tropes.name: Evil Laugh
tropes.html: Roger has one when he sings about Cruella.

tropes.name: Excellent Judge of Character
tropes.html: Roger is this towards Cruella. He is the one who invented the song "Cruella De Vil" after all. Just listen to the lyrics! Not to mention that he remembers how much Cruella wanted Pongo's and Perdita's puppies and how aggressive and angry she got when she couldn't have them. As such, he proclaims her to be his "number one suspect" after they're kidnapped, even after Anita argues against his accusations. Turns out he was right about this, even though he doesn't find out in the end.

tropes.name: Explosive Breeder
tropes.html: Played With. When all 101 dalmatians make their way back to the Radcliffe home, amid the reunion between human and canine, the family are shocked to find out that there are 99 puppies altogether. Roger, none the wiser about what really transpired, assumed that Pongo and Perdita had the other 84 puppies in their absence from home, summed up by the line: "Pongo, you ol' rascal!"

tropes.name: Failure Is the Only Option
tropes.html: Sadly, Cruella's obsession with the dalmatian fur coat she will never have ultimately lands her in this trope.

tropes.name: Failures on Ice
tropes.html: As the Colonel is trying to reach Cruella's mansion, he slips on the ice while trying to catch up with Pongo and Perdita.

tropes.name: Fat and Skinny
tropes.html: Jasper is tall and lanky while Horace is short and squat.

tropes.name: Filthy Fun
tropes.html: When the dogs are rolling in the soot to disguise themselves as black Labradors, they greatly enjoy it.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: One of the lines in the Cruella de Vil song — which is cut from the actual movie, but does appear in music video versions of the song — is "all innocent children had better beware". Roger had no idea how accurate that statement later turned out to be (well, if you're a dalmatian child, anyhow).

tropes.name: Fourth-Date Marriage
tropes.html: Let's do the math. The movie opens in spring. After Anita and Roger get married, they live together for six months, before the puppies are born in October. This places the wedding in April, so they must have married right after their Meet Cute.

tropes.name: Frame-Up
tropes.html: Cruella threatens to blame the entire puppy-napping/skinning scheme on Jasper and Horace to get them to finish the job.

tropes.name: Friend Not for Sale
tropes.html: Cruella De Vil desires to buy the litter of Dalmatian puppies so she can make them into a fur coat. However the Radcliffes firmly refuse and state the puppies are not for sale. This then leads her to attempt to kidnap said puppies.

tropes.name: "Friends" Rent Control
tropes.html: Roger and Anita are able to afford a pretty nice two-story home in London near Regent's Park, while also employing a nanny and keeping two dogs, despite Roger being something of a struggling songwriter while Anita's job (assuming she kept working after getting married) is never mentioned. It would seem the amount of Dalmatians finally forced them to relocate to the country in the sequel, funded by the success of Roger's song about Cruella.

tropes.name: Funny Phone Misunderstanding
tropes.html:
A similar even happens twice, in similar fashion both times -
  • When Cruella and Jasper are on the phone together, Jasper says, "Shut up, you idiot!" to Horace. Cruella responds with a Big "WHAT?!", and Jasper says, "No, not you, miss, I mean Horace!".
  • When Anita is on the phone with Cruella, the former accidentally calls Roger an idiot while still on the phone, offending Cruella who thought Anita was saying it to her.
  • In addition to these, when Jasper and Horace on calling Cruella, Horace is reading the newspaper while Jasper points out to Cruella that their crime is all over the papers. At this point Horace holds the phone up to his newspaper as if that will allow Cruella to see it.

tropes.name: Furry Reminder
tropes.html: Dogs can both speak and bark. In fact, in one scene, the Colonel has to translate a distant dog's barking into English so that the cat and horse he's talking to will understand.

tropes.name: Gender Flip
tropes.html: The character of Sergeant Tibbs (Tibb, in the novel) is changed in this adaptation from female to male. And on a more minor level, so is the puppy whose life Mr. Dearly/Roger saves at birth, given that this puppy is hinted to be Lucky — not Cadpig, as in the book.

tropes.name: Gondor Calls for Aid
tropes.html: Desperate to get the word out about the kidnapped puppies, Pongo resorts to the Twilight Bark, the local gossip chain. It works.

tropes.name: Good Smoking, Evil Smoking
tropes.html: Roger's Distinguished Gentleman's Pipe versus Cruella's cigarette with holder.

tropes.name: Goofy Print Underwear
tropes.html: Jasper's pink underwear gets exposed during the fight at the old house.

tropes.name: Go Through Me
tropes.html:
• Horace and Jasper corner the ninety-nine puppies in a room after Sergeant Tibs tried to help them escape. As the two men are approaching the puppies, Tibs has his arms stretched out as far as he can reach in front of the puppies in a desperate attempt to protect them from Horace and Jasper.
  • When the Dalmatians' Labrador ruse is exposed, the black Labrador charges at Horace and Jasper to give Pongo and Lucky enough time to get on the van.

tropes.name: Happily Adopted
tropes.html: Pongo and Perdita end up adopting the 84 orphaned puppies that they helped rescue. Fortunately, their owners agree, and the film ends with Roger saying they'll buy a large place in the country so the dogs will have plenty of room.

tropes.name: Happily Married
tropes.html: Roger and Anita, and by extension their pets Pongo and Perdita.

tropes.name: Heroic Dog
tropes.html: Pongo and Perdita not only rescue their kids, but also 84 more of them on realizing they have nowhere to go. All of the dogs that respond to the Twilight Bark end up proving to be this, especially those that go out of their way to help Perdita and Pongo find their puppies and then get home. The Great Dane gives Pongo and Perdita instructions on where to go while telling them to bark for help from his liaisons. While the Colonel doesn't do much physical stuff, he alerts Perdita and Pongo where the De Vil mansion is and distracts the Baduns as the dogs beat a retreat. A Rough Collie runs into the snow to get everyone to safety in the barn while fetching food scraps for the parents as the cows feed the little ones and make room for them in the hay. To top it all off, the Labrador helps arrange a ride for them in a truck and charges at Horace and Jasper when they and Cruella figure out the deception.

tropes.name: Horrible Judge of Character
tropes.html:
Anita honestly trusts Cruella, mainly due to them being old schoolmates, while no one else thinks very fondly of her at all.
Anita: Roger, I admit she's eccentric, but she's not a thief.
Roger: Well, she's still the number one suspect in my book!

tropes.name: Hyper-Competent Sidekick
tropes.html: Sergeant Tibbs and the Captain to the Colonel.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html: Cruella telling Horace and Jasper, "Watch your driving, you imbeciles! You wanna get nabbed by the police?!"

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
Nanny holds it firmly during the scene when Jasper and Horace abduct the puppies to an almost-comedic extent;
  • First, she tells them they're not coming in while Roger and Anita are gone, thusly informing the pair that she is the only one in the house.
  • Second, she threatens to call the police on them if they don't leave the house instead of just calling them immediately.
  • Third and most baffingly, after the puppies are gone, she wanders the streets pleading for anybody to call the police instead of just... calling them herself. It's a wonder her employment with Roger and Anita survived.

tropes.name: It Can Think
tropes.html: Discussed. Horace suggests that the dalmatians are just as smart as humans such as going up the creek to avoid leaving prints or rolling in soot to disguise themselves, but Jasper dismisses the notion.<!--* IDontLikeTheSoundOfThatPlace: Hell Hall.-->

tropes.name: I Don't Pay You to Think
tropes.html:
Horace comments "I've been thinking," and Jasper grabs him by the shirt and tells him that he's warned him about thinking. "I've got the knob for this job, so let's get on with it." They do this again later as they hunt the fleeing Dalmatians. They follow their tracks in the snow to a bridge over a frozen creek, only to become confused when the pawprints mysteriously stop. Unbeknownst to them, the Dalmatians are hiding from them under the bridge.
Horace: Jasper, I've been thinking—
Jasper: (sharply) Now, Horace!
Horace: (shining a flashlight down at the creek) But what if they went down the froze-up creek so as not to leave their tracks?
Jasper: (grabbing him by the shirt) Oh, Horace, you idiot! Dogs ain't that smart!

tropes.name: I'm Taking Her Home with Me!
tropes.html: Played for Drama and heartwarming feels. When Pongo tells his fifteen puppies that they're going home to London, Patch points out that the other puppies don't have homes and have nowhere to go. Pongo then immediately says they're taking everyone home and the humans will help, much to their delight. Roger on seeing the puppies decides they're getting a bigger place.

tropes.name: Internal Reveal
tropes.html: We know from the get-go that Cruella is behind the puppies' kidnapping, but Pongo and Perdita don't know about this until the Great Dane tells them about "the De Vil place" halfway through the film.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html: Cruella likes to make fun of Roger for being a Starving Artist in her opinion. Near the end, his first big hit as a musician turns out to be "The Villain Sucks" Song he wrote about her.

tropes.name: Janitor Impersonation Infiltration
